Automatic mail capture. At startup the module finds nodemailer transporters (providers, or fields of providers and controllers) and @nestjs-modules/mailer's MailerService, and records every message they send or fail to send: recipients, sender, subject, rendered HTML, text, attachments (names and sizes), status, error, duration, message id. watchers.mail now turns it off. See Mail. TelemetryMailWatcher.instrument() for senders created after startup; record() accepts nodemailer's options as they are and never throws. The Mail view shows the status, error, every address and attachment, and renders the HTML in a sandboxed frame with remote content blocked until you ask for it. Mail bodies are masked: JWTs and the query string of every link.

The access token is asked on every route of the dashboard. The guard compared the request path with basePath, so the dashboard and its API were served without the token for a case variant of the URL (/Telemetry/api/entries), under a global prefix without externalBasePath, with a basePath written without its leading slash (or the page with a trailing slash), when the two basePaths of forRootAsync differed, and on Fastify. It is now bound to the dashboard's controller and never looks at the path. Your routes that merely start with the same characters (/telemetryx) no longer answer 403, and a GraphQL resolver no longer fails in the guard once a token is set. The access token is compared in constant time. The JWT masking expression could take seconds on a body of JWT-like text, blocking the event loop for any client; it is now linear. A query value carrying a URL with a sensitive parameter (?next=https://app/reset?token=...) is now masked.

TelemetrySecurityGuard is no longer a global guard, and is constructed with the module options ({ accessToken }) instead of (basePath, accessToken). externalBasePath now only affects the request watcher.

The dashboard's JSON API is served under {basePath}/api, where the page calls it, so the dashboard shows data again. Credentials are masked in request bodies, query strings and headers, by name and JWT shape. The response body and headers are stored next to the request, masked like the request. An error code stays readable in recorded responses.
externalBasePath is honored by the access-token guard and the request watcher under a global prefix.

NestJS Telemetry is a Nest dynamic module plus a static page. Watchers write entries to a storage; a controller exposes the storage over HTTP; the page polls the controller.

TelemetryModule.forRoot() and forRootAsync() return the same global module: Options are resolved once: forRoot() merges them immediately, forRootAsync() in a factory provider. Every other provider reads the resolved TELEMETRY_OPTIONS, so both entry points behave identically. Storage is created by a factory from storage: SqliteTelemetryStorage(sqlitePath) or InMemoryTelemetryStorage(maxEntries). Global bindings: three interceptors, each built by a factory that returns a pass-through when its switch is off. Registration order is execution order: the request interceptor is outermost, so the context it creates is visible to the other two. Access token: TelemetrySecurityGuard is bound to TelemetryController with @UseGuards, not to the application, so it runs on the dashboard's routes only, wherever they are mounted, and reads the token from TELEMETRY_OPTIONS. Your routes never reach it. Passive watchers (log, schedule, event, mail) are providers your code injects. The mail instrumentation walks the providers at onApplicationBootstrap and instruments the mail senders it recognises. Routes: RouterModule.register() mounts TelemetryController at basePath; DiscoveryModule gives the mail instrumentation access to the providers. Exports: TELEMETRY_STORAGE, TELEMETRY_USER_PROVIDER and the four passive watchers. TELEMETRY_OPTIONS is not exported.

What the diagram implies: Anything that happens before the request interceptor (middleware, guards) has no batch and is not recorded as part of the request; a request rejected there is not recorded at all. Everything the handler does, including awaited work, runs inside TelemetryContext.run(), so its entries share the batch. See Batch correlation. The REQUEST entry is written last, when the response finishes, because only then is the status final.

The page polls three endpoints every five seconds (stats, filter options, and the current list) and fetches related entries when you open one. The controller is a thin layer over the storage interface: every read and write goes through TelemetryStorage, which is what makes the two storages interchangeable.

documents.s: Where to look in the code

documents.t: Every entry has a batchId. Entries recorded while handling the same HTTP request (or the same scheduled run) share it, which is how the dashboard shows "everything this request did" next to the request.

TelemetryContext wraps one AsyncLocalStorage<TelemetryStore>: interface TelemetryStore { batchId: string; userIdentifier?: string; tenantId?: string; } Method Does TelemetryContext.run(store, fn) Runs fn with store as the current context; everything fn starts asynchronously inherits it. getStore() The current store, or undefined. getBatchId(), getUserIdentifier(), getTenantId() Fields of the current store. getOrCreateBatchId() The current batch ID, or a new UUID. It does not enter a context. Watchers read the current store when they record. Outside any context the fields are ''.

The request interceptor creates one batch per HTTP request, with the user and tenant from req.user, and runs the rest of the chain (interceptors, pipes, handler) inside it. TelemetryScheduleWatcher.wrap() creates one batch per run. Mail keeps the batch of the code that called sendMail(), even when the transport answers later.

Work that does not start with an HTTP request (a queue consumer, a message handler, a CLI command) has no batch. Give it one so its entries group together: src/emails/email.consumer.ts import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'; import { TelemetryContext } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; @Injectable() export class EmailConsumer { async handle(job: { id: string; userEmail: string; data: unknown }) { return TelemetryContext.run({ batchId: randomUUID(), userIdentifier: job.userEmail }, () => this.process(job.data), ); } private async process(data: unknown) { // queries, logs and mail recorded here share the batch above } } The dashboard's related-entries list works for these batches too; there is just no REQUEST entry among them.

GET {basePath}/api/entries/:uuid/related returns every entry with the same batch ID as the given one, oldest first (an entry without a batch has no related entries). The detail panel lists them under Related entries (same request).

AsyncLocalStorage follows promises, timers and callbacks created inside the context. It does not follow work that was queued before the context existed and resumes later, such as a connection pool that calls back from the context of the request that opened the connection, or an event emitter whose listeners were attached elsewhere and that is driven by another source. Entries recorded there carry another batch, or none. The mail watcher handles the pool case itself; for the rest, run the work inside TelemetryContext.run() at the point where it starts. Also: Middleware, guards and exception filters run outside the request's context: their log lines are not linked to it. With watchers.requests: false no request context is created at all, so nothing recorded during requests carries a batch, user or tenant.

Masking happens before an entry is stored: what is masked never reaches the storage or the dashboard. It follows one principle, stated in the code: a dashboard that hides one field too many is a nuisance; one that shows a credential is a leak. Masked values become ***.

A key (header name, query parameter, JSON field at any depth) is first normalized: lower-cased, with spaces, ., _ and - removed. So X-Api-Key, new_password, refreshToken and card number all become comparable. It is sensitive when the normalized key: contains one of: password, passwd, passcode, secret, token, apikey, authorization, cardnumber, cvv, cvc, privatekey, credential, twofactor; or is exactly one of: code, otp, pin, pwd, pass, jwt, auth, bearer, cookie. The short names must match whole, because as substrings they would hit innocent keys (postcode, shipping, statusCode). Over-masking is accepted: tokenType is masked too. In responses, code is not in the list: a server's code is nearly always an error or status code ({"code":"401"}), so it stays readable. A verification code in a response is still caught by the other names or by its shape.
documents.s: How a key is judged sensitive

documents.t: Part Rule Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie Always ***. Any other header with a sensitive name *** (x-api-key, x-auth-token...). Location, Content-Location, Referer, Refresh The query string and fragment of the URL are masked like a query string. Query string Pair by pair: a sensitive key gets ***; so does a value that is itself a URL or query string containing a sensitive key (?next=https://app/reset?token=...). JSON body Every sensitive field at any depth, arrays included. A string value that holds a JSON document is parsed and masked field by field. Any other string value has its JWTs masked. Text body Parsed as JSON when it is JSON. Otherwise JWTs are masked, and if the text mentions a sensitive name (password=...) the whole body becomes ***. Binary body (Buffer) Not stored: [binary body omitted]. Bodies are masked first and cut at 10,000 characters afterwards, so truncation never exposes half of a masked value.

The response body is captured only when it is text (JSON, XML, text/* except event streams), uncompressed, not UTF-16/32 and at most 256 KB; then masked with the same rules as a request body (minus code) and cut at 10,000 characters. Response headers follow the header rules above, Set-Cookie included. See Requests for the capture rules.

A signed JWT is recognised by its shape: three base64url parts where the first two start with eyJ. It is masked in JSON string values, text bodies and mail, even under an innocent key or in free text. The match only starts where a run of base64url characters starts, so it stays fast on hostile input.

A mail body has no field names, so it is masked by shape: JWTs, and the query string and fragment of every URL in it, href attributes included (https://app/reset?token=... keeps the address and loses the token). The subject is masked for JWTs. See Mail.

warning These are stored as they are. Keep them in mind before you run the dashboard where others can see it, or with real users' data. URL paths: /orders/track/:token keeps its token. Header values and query values under innocent names, JWTs included: x-session: eyJ... or ?state=eyJ... are stored as sent. Exception messages and stack traces. SQL and its parameters (TypeORM), and Prisma arguments and data: a password hash or a token bound to a query is visible. Log messages, contexts and traces. Event payloads. Model data: changed fields (TypeORM) and written data (Prisma). Cache keys. Mail addresses, and codes written in the text of a mail ("your code is 123456"). User identifiers: the request's user is identified by email first, so email addresses appear in every entry's userIdentifier. Masking hides credentials, not personal data. Treat the dashboard as holding production-grade personal data whenever it records real traffic.

interface TelemetryEntry { uuid: string; // unique id type: TelemetryEntryType; // one of the nine types createdAt: Date; // when it was recorded batchId: string; // request or run it belongs to, or '' content: Record<string, any>; userIdentifier: string; // or '' tenantId: string; // or '' tags: string[]; } TelemetryEntryType is a string enum: REQUEST, EXCEPTION, QUERY, LOG, SCHEDULE, CACHE, EVENT, MAIL, MODEL. The SQLite storage keeps content and tags as JSON text and createdAt as an ISO-8601 string, and turns them back into objects and a Date when it reads. The in-memory storage keeps the objects themselves, and returns them by reference: treat entries you read as read-only.

Field Type Notes method string uri string Path (Express req.path) queryString string Masked status number Final status duration number ms ipAddress string contentType, responseContentType string requestHeaders, responseHeaders object Masked requestBody, responseBody string Masked, at most 10,000 characters Tags: none.

Field Type Notes class string Constructor name message string Not masked trace string At most 5,000 characters file, line, location string First stack frame uri, method string The request cause string String(error.cause) Tags: exception:<Class>.
TypeORM: sql, type (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL/OTHER), duration, parameters. Prisma: model, action, type, duration, args, error. Tags: query:<type>.
level (LOG/ERROR/WARN/DEBUG/VERBOSE), message, context, trace. Tags: log:<level>.
class, method, status (completed/failed), duration, exception. Tags: schedule:<status>.
operation (HIT/MISS), cacheName (''), key, duration. Tags: cache:<operation>.
event, eventClass, payload, handlerClass, handlerMethod. Tags: event:<name>.

Always: to, from, subject, type, bodyPreview, status (sent/failed), source. When present: cc, bcc, replyTo, html, htmlTruncated, text, template, attachments ({ filename, contentType, size? }[]), error, duration, messageId, accepted, rejected, transport. Tags: mail, to:<address> per recipient, mail:failed.
TypeORM: entity, action (CREATED/UPDATED/DELETED), entityId, changedFields. Prisma: entity, action, entityId, data. Tags: model:<action>, entity:<Name>.

The storage is injectable through TELEMETRY_STORAGE, so you can store entries of the existing types yourself, as the Cache and Prisma recipes do. Use one of the nine types (the dashboard has no view for others), check storage.isEnabled() first, read the batch from TelemetryContext, and keep content JSON-serializable: no BigInt, no cycles.

basePath is the path the module registers its controller at, through RouterModule. app.setGlobalPrefix() is applied on top of every registered route afterwards, so with a global prefix the dashboard is no longer where basePath says.

main.ts basePath Dashboard page JSON API no prefix /telemetry /telemetry /telemetry/api/... app.setGlobalPrefix('api') /telemetry /api/telemetry /api/telemetry/api/... app.setGlobalPrefix('api/v1') /admin/telemetry /api/v1/admin/telemetry /api/v1/admin/telemetry/api/... The page finds its API by itself: it takes the path it was served from, drops a trailing slash and appends /api. Nothing needs configuring for the page to work under a prefix.

The request watcher skips the dashboard's own calls, so they do not fill the Requests view. It recognises them by their path: the ones that start with externalBasePath when it is set, and with basePath otherwise. Under a prefix, requests carry /api/telemetry/..., which does not start with /telemetry, so without externalBasePath every call the dashboard makes (three every five seconds) is recorded as a request. The access token does not depend on it. The guard is bound to the dashboard's routes, so the token is asked under the prefix with or without externalBasePath (see Where the token is checked). Set externalBasePath to the full path: src/app.module.ts TelemetryModule.forRoot({ basePath: '/telemetry', externalBasePath: '/api/telemetry', accessToken: process.env.TELEMETRY_TOKEN ?? '', }); src/main.ts app.setGlobalPrefix('api'); Write both values with a leading slash and without a trailing one: the request watcher compares them as plain string prefixes.

Instead of following the prefix, you can exclude the dashboard routes from it. Requests then carry basePath again, and externalBasePath is not needed: src/main.ts import { RequestMethod } from '@nestjs/common'; app.setGlobalPrefix('api', { exclude: [ { path: 'telemetry', method: RequestMethod.ALL }, { path: 'telemetry/(.*)', method: RequestMethod.ALL }, ], }); The dashboard stays at /telemetry while the rest of the app moves to /api. On NestJS 11 the (.*) wildcard is the legacy syntax: Nest converts it and logs a deprecation warning; the new form is telemetry/*path.

documents.t: ignoredPrefixes is compared with the path as requests carry it, prefix included. With app.setGlobalPrefix('api'), write /api/health, not /health.
When a reverse proxy rewrites paths, the browser's address no longer matches what the app sees. The page then needs to be told where its API is: see Serving and embedding the dashboard.

documents.t: TelemetryModule.forRoot(options) and the factory of forRootAsync() take a TelemetryModuleOptions object. Every property is optional; the defaults come from DEFAULT_OPTIONS in packages/core/src/telemetry.options.ts.

Option Type Default What it does storage 'memory' | 'sqlite' 'memory' Where entries are kept. Any value other than 'sqlite' selects memory. See Storage. sqlitePath string '.telemetry.db' Path of the SQLite database file, relative to the process's working directory. Used only with storage: 'sqlite'. basePath string '/telemetry' Path the dashboard page is served at; the JSON API is under {basePath}/api. Write it with a leading slash and no trailing slash. externalBasePath string basePath The dashboard path as requests really carry it, when a global prefix is applied on top of basePath. Read by the request watcher, to leave the dashboard's own calls out of the recorded requests. It plays no part in the access token. See Global prefix. maxEntries number 1000 Most entries kept per type by the in-memory storage; the oldest is dropped when a new one arrives. Ignored by SQLite. pruneHours number 24 Entries older than this many hours are deleted by the periodic prune. pruneIntervalMs number 3600000 How often the periodic prune runs (1 hour). accessToken string '' When non-empty, the dashboard and its API require this token. See Access token and security. ignoredPrefixes string[] ['/health', '/swagger', '/api-docs'] Requests whose path starts with one of these strings are not recorded. A plain string prefix: /health also skips /healthcare. basePackage string '' When set, the log watcher records only log lines whose context starts with this string. See Logs. flushIntervalMs number 2000 How often buffered entries are written to SQLite. watchers TelemetryWatcherOptions all true Per-watcher switches, below.

Option Default Effect today requests true false replaces the request interceptor with a pass-through. exceptions true false replaces the exception interceptor with a pass-through. cache true false replaces the cache interceptor with a pass-through. mail true false turns off mail discovery and makes TelemetryMailWatcher record nothing. queries true Not read by any package. models true Not read by any package. logs true Not read: the log watcher records whatever it is given. schedules true Not read. events true Not read. Watcher toggles explains each switch and how to turn off the ones that are not read.

The options you pass are spread over DEFAULT_OPTIONS, and watchers is spread over the default watchers. A key you leave out keeps its default. A key present with the value undefined replaces the default with undefined; see Async configuration for what that breaks. Numbers are not validated: 0, negative values and NaN are used as given. Options are read once, at startup.
src/app.module.ts TelemetryModule.forRoot({ maxEntries: 500, ignoredPrefixes: ['/health', '/metrics'], watchers: { cache: false }, });

src/app.module.ts TelemetryModule.forRoot({ storage: 'sqlite', sqlitePath: 'var/telemetry.db', pruneHours: 72, pruneIntervalMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, flushIntervalMs: 1000, }); Add var/telemetry.db* to .gitignore: WAL mode creates -wal and -shm files next to the database.

src/main.ts app.setGlobalPrefix('api/v1'); src/app.module.ts TelemetryModule.forRoot({ accessToken: process.env.TELEMETRY_TOKEN ?? '', externalBasePath: '/api/v1/telemetry', ignoredPrefixes: ['/api/v1/health'], }); The dashboard is then at /api/v1/telemetry?token=.... Note that ignoredPrefixes is compared with the full path, prefix included.

documents.t: The dashboard and its JSON API show everything the watchers record: request and response bodies, headers, SQL, mail, user identifiers. They can also pause recording and delete entries. The accessToken option is the only access control the package provides. This page explains how it works, where it stops, and what to add around it.

The module serves two things under the dashboard path (basePath, /telemetry by default): Route What it is GET {basePath} The dashboard page: static HTML, no data in it {basePath}/api/... The JSON API the page calls: entries, related entries, stats, status, filters, tags, memory, and the routes that change state: POST /api/toggle, POST /api/flush, POST /api/prune, POST /api/prune/expired and DELETE /api/entries The full list is in the REST API reference. When accessToken is set, every one of these routes requires it. When it is not set, none does.

Pass the token from your environment, never from source code: app.module.ts import { Module } from '@nestjs/common'; import { TelemetryModule } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; @Module({ imports: [ TelemetryModule.forRoot({ accessToken: process.env.TELEMETRY_TOKEN, }), ], }) export class AppModule {} warning If TELEMETRY_TOKEN is not set, accessToken is undefined, the dashboard is open, and nothing tells you so. Outside your own machine, read the token so that a missing value stops the app from starting. With @nestjs/config, getOrThrow() does that: app.module.ts import { Module } from '@nestjs/common'; import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config'; import { TelemetryModule } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; @Module({ imports: [ ConfigModule.forRoot(), TelemetryModule.forRootAsync({ imports: [ConfigModule], inject: [ConfigService], useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => ({ accessToken: config.getOrThrow<string>('TELEMETRY_TOKEN'), }), }), ], }) export class AppModule {} See Async configuration for the rest of forRootAsync. Use a long random value made of URL-safe ASCII characters, so it travels in a query string and in a header without any encoding: node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('hex'))" The token is read once, when the module starts. To rotate it, change the value and restart the app.

Add the token to the dashboard address: http://localhost:3000/telemetry?token=<your-token> The page reads token from its own address and sends it as the x-telemetry-token header on every API call it makes. It never adds the token to the API URLs. Moving between views does not change the page address, so the token stays for the whole session, and a reload keeps it. Opening the page without the token answers 403 with Nest's default body ({"message":"Forbidden resource","error":"Forbidden","statusCode":403}); there is no login form. Scripts and other API clients send the same header: curl -H "x-telemetry-token: $TELEMETRY_TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/telemetry/api/status The token query parameter is accepted on the API routes too, but the header keeps the token out of access logs. If you serve the page from another location (see Serving and embedding the dashboard), it still takes the token from the token parameter of its own address.
documents.s: Open the dashboard with the token

documents.t: TelemetrySecurityGuard is bound to the dashboard's controller with @UseGuards, not to your whole application. Nest runs it on exactly the requests it routes to the dashboard page and its API, and on nothing else. It never looks at the path: whatever spelling, case, global prefix, mount point or HTTP adapter brought the request there, the same check applies. What that means in practice, with the token T and the default basePath: Request Result GET /telemetry 403 GET /telemetry?token=T 200 GET /telemetry/api/stats with x-telemetry-token: T 200 GET /telemetry/api/stats?token=T 200 GET /Telemetry/api/stats, a case variant Express routes to the dashboard 403 GET /telemetry/api/stats with Authorization: Bearer T 403: the Authorization header is not read GET /telemetry/api/stats?token=T&token=T 403: a repeated parameter arrives as a list, not a string GET /telemetry-reports, one of your routes not checked GET /orders not checked The comparison is exact and case-sensitive. It runs in constant time, on digests of both values, so the response time shows neither how much of a guess was right nor how long the token is. The header name is not case-sensitive (Node lower-cases header names); its value must match exactly. The query parser decodes the parameter before the comparison: + becomes a space and %2B a plus sign. A hex token avoids the question. TelemetrySecurityGuard is exported from @nestjs-telemetry/core, but you never need to register it: the dashboard's controller already uses it. It reads accessToken from the module options.

accessToken defaults to ''. With an empty or missing token the guard lets every request through. The page and every API route then answer to anyone who can reach your app, including the routes that pause recording, prune and delete entries. That is fine on a laptop where nobody else can reach the port. Set a token everywhere else, shared development and staging environments included. Even on your own machine, an open dashboard cannot tell your requests from the ones another web page makes your browser send to localhost.

On every route of the dashboard, wherever it is mounted. None of these settings changes that: A global prefix. With app.setGlobalPrefix('api/v1') the dashboard moves to /api/v1/telemetry, and the token is asked there, with no other setting. externalBasePath plays no part in the token; it only keeps the dashboard's own calls out of the recorded requests (see Global prefix and externalBasePath). forRootAsync with a custom path. The routes are mounted with the basePath you pass next to useFactory, or at /telemetry when you pass none. A basePath returned by the factory does not move them. Wherever they end up, the token is asked there: basePath next to useFactory basePath returned by useFactory Dashboard served at not set not set /telemetry /admin/telemetry /admin/telemetry /admin/telemetry not set /admin/telemetry /telemetry /admin/telemetry not set /admin/telemetry Pass the same value in both places anyway: the request watcher uses the one the factory returns to recognise the dashboard's own calls. The spelling of the path. basePath: 'telemetry', without its leading slash, and basePath: '/telemetry/', with a trailing slash, both serve the dashboard at /telemetry, behind the token. Write it with a leading slash and without a trailing one all the same, for the request watcher's sake. Case variants. Express routes without regard to case, so /TELEMETRY/api/entries reaches the dashboard API. It goes through the same check. Fastify. The guard reads only the token query parameter and the x-telemetry-token header, which a Fastify request has too. The package's test suite runs on the Express adapter only. Your own routes never reach the guard, including the ones whose path starts with the same characters as the dashboard's: /telemetry-reports and /telemetryx answer as if the module were not there.

Nest runs every global guard on every route, the dashboard routes included, and a request goes through only when all of them allow it. That has consequences in both directions: An app-wide JWT guard blocks the dashboard. A browser does not add Authorization: Bearer ... to a page it opens, and the dashboard's API calls only add x-telemetry-token. You get 401 from your guard, even with the right telemetry token. A 401 means another guard refused the request; TelemetrySecurityGuard answers 403. A guard that authenticates with a cookie (a session) lets the dashboard work for users who are logged in: the browser sends the cookie with the page and with the API calls, which are same-origin. Those users need both your session and the telemetry token. A global rate limiter such as ThrottlerGuard counts the dashboard's polling: an open tab calls three API routes every five seconds. Exclude the dashboard path from it (@nestjs/throttler has a skipIf option) or allow for that rate. To let the dashboard through a JWT guard, skip your check on the dashboard path and leave the token to TelemetrySecurityGuard. The dashboard controller is not part of the package's public exports, so a @Public()-style decorator cannot be put on it; match the request path instead: jwt-auth.guard.ts import { ExecutionContext, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; import { AuthGuard } from '@nestjs/passport'; // The dashboard path as requests carry it, global prefix included. const TELEMETRY_PATH = '/telemetry'; function isTelemetryRequest(context: ExecutionContext): boolean { if (context.getType() !== 'http') return false; const path: string = context.switchToHttp().getRequest().path ?? ''; return path === TELEMETRY_PATH || path.startsWith(`${TELEMETRY_PATH}/`); } @Injectable() export class JwtAuthGuard extends AuthGuard('jwt') { canActivate(context: ExecutionContext) { // TelemetrySecurityGuard checks the access token on these paths. if (isTelemetryRequest(context)) return true; return super.canActivate(context); } } danger Skip your guard on the dashboard path only when accessToken is set. Without a token, your guard was the only thing in front of the dashboard. Keep the / boundary of the comparison, as above, so that none of your own routes that merely start with the same characters (/telemetry-reports) skips your guard. A case variant of the dashboard path that the comparison does not match still has to pass your guard, and then the telemetry token, so it opens nothing.

Keep the dashboard off the public internet. Allow the dashboard path only from your VPN or office network at the reverse proxy or ingress, with a rule that matches regardless of case. The token is a second line, not the only one. Serve it over HTTPS only. The token travels in a header and in the page address. Keep the token out of logs. The page address carries ?token=, so your proxy, ingress and HTTP logging middleware record it. Mask the token parameter in those logs. The request watcher leaves the dashboard's own calls out, and masks a token parameter wherever it records one. Consider letting your proxy hold the token. The guard accepts the header on the page request too. A proxy that authenticates your team (single sign-on) and adds x-telemetry-token to every request under the dashboard path means the browser never sees the token: open the page without ?token=, and the proxy supplies the header on each API call as well. Remember what one token grants. There are no users, roles or read-only access, and no audit of who looked: anyone with the token can read every entry, pause recording and delete entries. Rate-limit the dashboard path at the proxy; the guard has no lockout. Know what the page loads. The dashboard page loads Tailwind CSS from cdn.tailwindcss.com and Alpine.js from cdn.jsdelivr.net, without integrity attributes. Those scripts run with access to the page, the token in its address and every entry it shows. Treat what is stored as sensitive. Masking hides credentials, not personal data; see Data masking for what is stored as is.

Entries go to one storage, chosen with the storage option. Both implement the same TelemetryStorage interface, so the dashboard and the watchers behave the same on either; the differences are durability, limits and cost. 'memory' (default) 'sqlite' Survives a restart No Yes Size limit maxEntries per type None besides pruning Write path Immediate Buffered, flushed every flushIntervalMs Shared between processes No One file per process; not designed for several writers Native module No better-sqlite3

InMemoryTelemetryStorage keeps one array per entry type, newest first. When a type already holds maxEntries entries, storing a new one drops the oldest of that type. Nothing is written anywhere: a restart starts empty, and each instance of a scaled-out app has its own entries. Reads filter the arrays directly: userIdentifier and tenantId must be equal (strict comparison). method compares content.method, ignoring case; statusGroup (2xx...5xx) compares the hundreds of content.status. Entries without those fields never match. search matches, ignoring case, any top-level value of content converted with String(). A nested object becomes [object Object], so text inside headers, payloads or arguments is not found. Pages are cut after filtering, so the total and the pages agree. note Each type is capped separately: the default allows up to 9,000 entries in total. A REQUEST entry can hold two bodies of up to 10 KB each and its headers; a MAIL entry up to 50 KB of HTML. Budget memory accordingly.

SqliteTelemetryStorage uses better-sqlite3 with WAL journaling and synchronous = NORMAL. It creates one table on first use: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS telemetry_entries ( uuid TEXT PRIMARY KEY, type TEXT NOT NULL, created_at TEXT NOT NULL, batch_id TEXT NOT NULL, content TEXT NOT NULL, user_identifier TEXT NOT NULL, tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL, tags TEXT NOT NULL ); -- plus one index each on type, created_at, batch_id, user_identifier and tenant_id content and tags are stored as JSON text and created_at as an ISO-8601 string; reads turn them back into objects and Dates.

Storing an entry only appends it to an in-process buffer. The buffer is written to the database: every flushIntervalMs (2 seconds by default), by the pruner service; before every listing, count, related-entries, tags or filter-options read, so the dashboard always sees what was stored; when the module is destroyed (app.close()); on POST {basePath}/api/flush. A flush writes up to 200 entries per transaction, repeating until the buffer is empty. INSERT OR IGNORE makes a replayed entry harmless. Filters on userIdentifier and tenantId run in SQL. The others (method, statusGroup, search) run in JavaScript after loading every row of the type. Current limitation Filtered reads load the whole type. With a method, status or search filter, each dashboard refresh reads and parses every stored row of that type, twice (page and total). better-sqlite3 is synchronous, so on a large database this blocks your application's event loop for seconds. Keep the database small with pruning. One unserialisable entry stops all writes. If an entry's content cannot be turned into JSON (a BigInt, for example a Prisma or TypeORM bigint id), its batch is put back in the buffer and every later flush fails on it: nothing more is written, reads answer 500, the buffer grows, and app.close() rejects. No size limit. maxEntries does not apply; only pruning removes rows. The connection is never closed by the module at shutdown.

TelemetryPrunerService starts two timers when the module is created: Timer Interval Does Prune pruneIntervalMs (1 h) Deletes every entry created more than pruneHours (24) hours ago, buffer included. Flush flushIntervalMs (2 s) Writes the SQLite buffer (does nothing in memory). On app.close() both timers are cleared and the buffer is flushed. Errors in either timer are logged and do not stop it. You can also prune on demand: POST {basePath}/api/prune?hours=N deletes entries older than N hours (hours=0 is treated as 24), and the dashboard's Prune button calls it with 24 hours. See the REST API. note The timers are not unref()ed: a script that creates an application context and never closes it does not exit on its own. Call app.close().

Use memory for local development and tests: nothing to clean up, and the cap keeps memory bounded. Use SQLite when entries must survive restarts (a staging server, a long debugging session), with a pruneHours that keeps the file small, and keep its files out of version control: .gitignore .telemetry.db* Neither storage is shared between instances; to look at several instances, open each one's dashboard. A third-party storage cannot be plugged in through options today: see Custom storage.

watchers holds one boolean per entry type. All default to true. They do not all work the same way, because the watchers are not all wired the same way: Bound interceptors (requests, exceptions, cache) run on every HTTP request. Their switch replaces the interceptor with a pass-through. Mail is instrumented automatically at startup. Its switch skips the instrumentation and makes the mail watcher record nothing. Passive helpers (logs, schedules, events) record only what your code hands them. They are always registered, and their switch is not read. ORM watchers (queries, models) live in the TypeORM and Prisma packages, which do not read the core options.

Switch Read by Effect of false requests core module No REQUEST entries, and no batch context: see the warning below. exceptions core module No EXCEPTION entries. cache core module No CACHE entries. mail core module No mail sender is instrumented; TelemetryMailWatcher.record() and instrument() do nothing. logs nothing None. schedules nothing None. events nothing None. queries nothing None. models nothing None. Current limitation logs, schedules, events, queries and models have no effect. To turn one of those off, do not wire it: do not install TelemetryLogWatcher as a logger, do not call TelemetryScheduleWatcher.wrap() or TelemetryEventWatcher.record(), do not import TelemetryTypeOrmModule or register the Prisma middlewares. Current limitation The request interceptor is also what starts the batch context of a request (batch ID, user, tenant). With requests: false, entries recorded during a request (queries, logs, mail, exceptions) no longer carry a batch ID or the user and tenant. To stop recording requests but keep correlation, leave requests on and add the paths you do not want to ignoredPrefixes; note that an ignored path gets no batch context either.

In forRoot({ watchers: { requests: undefined } }), or a factory that returns undefined for a switch, the value replaces the default. For requests, exceptions and cache that means off; mail treats undefined as on. Give every switch a boolean.

The switches are read once, at startup. To stop recording while the app runs, use the dashboard's Enabled button (or POST {basePath}/api/toggle): it pauses every watcher at once, since each one checks the storage's recording flag before storing. Entries already recorded stay. See Using the dashboard.
The project lives at github.com/sergiodm92/nestjs-telemetry. Issues and pull requests are welcome.

nestjs-telemetry/ ├── package.json npm workspaces root (packages/*) ├── tsconfig.base.json shared compiler options (ES2022, CommonJS, strict, decorators) ├── packages/ │ ├── core/ @nestjs-telemetry/core │ │ ├── src/ │ │ │ ├── telemetry.module.ts forRoot / forRootAsync, bindings │ │ │ ├── telemetry.options.ts options and defaults │ │ │ ├── controller/ REST API │ │ │ ├── storage/ interface, in-memory, SQLite │ │ │ ├── context/ AsyncLocalStorage context, user provider │ │ │ ├── watchers/ every watcher, the guard, mail instrumentation │ │ │ ├── pruner/ prune and flush timers │ │ │ └── dashboard/index.html the dashboard (Alpine.js + Tailwind) │ │ └── test/ unit and HTTP-level specs, test/support harness │ ├── typeorm/ @nestjs-telemetry/typeorm (subscribers + module) │ └── prisma/ @nestjs-telemetry/prisma (middlewares) └── website/ this documentation (Docusaurus), not an npm workspace

Node.js 20 or later is needed to develop (the test suite uses nodemailer 10). npm install # every workspace npm test --workspaces # all test suites npm run build --workspaces # tsc, plus copying the dashboard HTML into core/dist npm run lint --workspaces # tsc --noEmit Per package: cd packages/core && npm test cd packages/typeorm && npx jest cd packages/prisma && npx jest The TypeORM and Prisma packages resolve @nestjs-telemetry/core to packages/core/src through Jest's moduleNameMapper, so they test against the current core source.

Telemetry observes, it never acts. A watcher must not change arguments, results, errors or responses, and must not throw into the host. Catch failures where recording happens. Check storage.isEnabled() before doing any recording work. Mask by name, then by shape. New data paths go through the masking helpers in watchers/request.interceptor.ts. When in doubt, mask. Bound everything. Truncate stored text, cap lists, and keep scans of untrusted input linear: no regular expression that can backtrack over a long input. Test behavior, against a real app. HTTP-level specs use test/support/test-app.ts, which builds a real Nest application with supertest. Prefer asserting on what the dashboard API returns over internal state. The dashboard's API contract is pinned by test/dashboard.contract.spec.ts: every API call the page makes must exist on the controller.

Add or reuse a TelemetryEntryType and decide the entry's content fields and tags. Write the watcher in packages/core/src/watchers/: it takes the storage, reads the batch from TelemetryContext, checks isEnabled(), and never throws into the host. Wire it in buildWatcherProviders() in telemetry.module.ts, honoring its watchers.* switch, and export it from src/index.ts if users call it. In dashboard/index.html: the list row, the detail panel, getGroupKey() and getEntrySummary(), using exactly the field names the watcher writes. Specs: the watcher on its own, and through a real app. Documentation: a page under website/docs/watchers/ and the entry model.

Each package has a prepublishOnly script that builds it; core's build copies src/dashboard/index.html into dist/dashboard/, which the controller serves. Each package ships dist and its own LICENSE. Bump the ORM packages' @nestjs-telemetry/core peer range when core's major or minor changes.

The site is a Docusaurus project in website/, outside the npm workspaces: cd website npm install npm start # dev server with live reload npm run build # static site in website/build; fails on broken links npm run serve # serve the build locally Pages are plain Markdown in website/docs/, the sidebar is website/sidebars.ts. Write what the code does today, and state limitations plainly in a :::warning[Current limitation] block. The site is published at https://sergiodm92.github.io/nestjs-telemetry/ by the Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml): on every push to main that changes website/, it builds the site and pushes website/build to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves.

GET {basePath} answers with dist/dashboard/index.html from the package, read from disk on each request and sent with the Express response API (res.type('text/html').send(...)). It is plain HTML with an Alpine.js app inline; there is no build step and no server-side rendering.

The page computes its API base when it loads: const base = window.__TELEMETRY_BASE_PATH__ || window.location.pathname.replace(/\/+$/, ''); const apiBase = base + '/api'; So by default the API is "the path this page was served from, plus /api". That follows any basePath and any global prefix with no configuration. If your setup serves the page under a different path than the API (a proxy that rewrites one but not the other), define window.__TELEMETRY_BASE_PATH__ before the page's script runs, for example from a page of your own that embeds a copy of the HTML.
The page reads token from its own query string and sends it as the x-telemetry-token header on every API call. It never puts the token in API URLs. See Access token and security.

Asset From Tailwind CSS (play CDN script, unpinned) https://cdn.tailwindcss.com Alpine.js 3.14.9 https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/alpinejs@3.14.9/dist/cdn.min.js Neither has an integrity attribute. Consequences: No internet, no dashboard: on an offline machine the page loads unstyled and inert. Content-Security-Policy: the page needs inline scripts, Alpine's eval-based expressions, styles injected by Tailwind, and both CDN hosts. A strict policy (helmet's default, for example) leaves it blank. Relax the policy for the dashboard path only: src/main.ts import helmet from 'helmet'; const strict = helmet(); const forDashboard = helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: { directives: { 'script-src': ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'", "'unsafe-eval'", 'https://cdn.tailwindcss.com', 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net'], 'style-src': ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'"], }, }, }); app.use((req, res, next) => (req.path.startsWith('/telemetry') ? forDashboard : strict)(req, res, next));

Proxy the dashboard path and everything under it to the app unchanged and the page works as is. If the proxy rewrites paths (/tools/telemetry outside, /telemetry inside), the page computes its API from the outside path, which the proxy also forwards, so it keeps working as long as both the page and /api/... go through the same rewrite. Restrict the path to your network at the proxy, with a rule that ignores case.

Many apps register a global interceptor that wraps responses, as in the NestJS documentation's TransformInterceptor: return next.handle().pipe(map((data) => ({ data }))); That interceptor also wraps the telemetry API, whose answers already have their own envelope ({ success, message, data }). The page then finds its data one level too deep and shows nothing. Let the telemetry controller through: src/common/transform.interceptor.ts import { CallHandler, ExecutionContext, Injectable, NestInterceptor } from '@nestjs/common'; import { map } from 'rxjs/operators'; @Injectable() export class TransformInterceptor implements NestInterceptor { intercept(context: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler) { // The telemetry dashboard expects its controller's own envelope. if (context.getClass().name === 'TelemetryController') return next.handle(); return next.handle().pipe(map((data) => ({ data }))); } } The controller class is not exported by the package, so compare its name, or the request path. The same applies to anything else that rewrites responses for every route: serializers, response-shaping filters, or a global ClassSerializerInterceptor with options that change plain objects.

The dashboard is a single page served by your application at basePath (/telemetry by default). It reads everything through the REST API and refreshes on its own every five seconds. If you set an access token, open it as /telemetry?token=<token>; the page sends the token with every call it makes.

Sidebar: the home view and one view per entry type (Requests, Exceptions, Queries, Logs, Schedule, Cache, Events, Mail, Models), each with its count. At the bottom, Recording or Paused. Top bar of a list view: the user and tenant filters, the method and status filters (Requests only), the search box, and the Auto, Grouped, Enabled and Clear all buttons. Detail panel: opens on the right when you click an entry.
One card per entry type with its count (click a card to open the view), a Prune entries older than 24h button, and the ten most recent requests.

Each view lists the entries of one type, newest first, 50 per page; when there are more, a pager shows "Showing 1-50 of N". View Each row shows Requests Method, path, status (colored by class), duration, time Exceptions Class, message, location and method Queries Statement type and the SQL (first 120 characters) Logs Level and message Schedule Class, method, status, duration Cache Operation, cache name, key, duration Events Event name Mail A FAILED badge when it failed, subject, recipients, time Models Action, entity, id, changed fields

User and Tenant list every user identifier and tenant id recorded so far, and filter every view by them. Method and Status (2xx...5xx) filter requests. Search matches, ignoring case, any top-level field of an entry's content. It runs 300 ms after you stop typing. Nested data (headers, payloads, arguments) is not searched. Changing view resets the search and the method and status filters; the user and tenant filters stay.

With Grouped on (the default), identical entries are folded into one row with a xN badge; click the badge to expand the group. What counts as identical depends on the type: Type Grouped by Request Method, path and status Exception Class and message Query SQL Log Level, logger and message Schedule Class and method Cache Operation, cache name and key Event Event name and payload class Mail Subject and recipients Model Action, entity class and id Grouping is applied to the current page only.

The panel shows the content of the entry in sections suited to its type: headers and bodies of a request, the stack of an exception, the formatted SQL of a query, the rendered HTML of a mail, and so on. Copy buttons put a section on the clipboard. Below, Related entries (same request) lists everything recorded with the same batch ID: the queries, logs, mail and exceptions of that request, in the order they happened. Click one to open it. The panel ends with the entry's UUID, time, batch ID and tags.

Control What it does Auto Turns the five-second refresh on and off. Grouped Turns grouping on and off. Enabled / Disabled Pauses or resumes recording for the whole application (POST /api/toggle). Paused watchers store nothing; existing entries stay. Clear all After a confirmation, deletes every entry of the current view's type (DELETE /api/entries?type=...). Prune entries older than 24h Deletes entries older than 24 hours, whatever pruneHours is (POST /api/prune?hours=24).

Current limitation The page does not read the recording state when it loads: it shows Enabled/Recording even if recording was paused, and the first click then reports the real state. After a search or a clear, the page number is kept, so you can land on an empty page with no pager; change view to reset it. Some fields are not shown: a log's context and stack, an event's handler, a model's entity name in the detail panel. Prisma queries appear as blank rows in the Queries view. The data is in the entry (see it through the API). Copy buttons need a secure context: they work on localhost and over HTTPS, not on plain HTTP to another host. A slow answer for a previous view or page can briefly replace the current one.

TelemetryModule.forRootAsync() builds the options with a factory, so you can read them from ConfigService or any other provider. It registers exactly the same providers, watchers and routes as forRoot().

TelemetryModule.forRootAsync({ imports?: any[]; // modules the factory's dependencies come from inject?: any[]; // tokens handed to useFactory, in order useFactory: (...args) => TelemetryModuleOptions | Promise<TelemetryModuleOptions>; basePath?: string; // where the dashboard and its API are mounted });

src/app.module.ts import { Module } from '@nestjs/common'; import { ConfigModule, ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config'; import { TelemetryModule, TelemetryModuleOptions } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; const TELEMETRY_PATH = '/telemetry'; @Module({ imports: [ ConfigModule.forRoot(), TelemetryModule.forRootAsync({ basePath: TELEMETRY_PATH, imports: [ConfigModule], inject: [ConfigService], useFactory: (config: ConfigService): TelemetryModuleOptions => ({ basePath: TELEMETRY_PATH, storage: config.get('TELEMETRY_STORAGE') === 'sqlite' ? 'sqlite' : 'memory', sqlitePath: config.get('TELEMETRY_SQLITE_PATH', '.telemetry.db'), accessToken: config.get('TELEMETRY_TOKEN', ''), pruneHours: Number(config.get('TELEMETRY_PRUNE_HOURS', 24)), }), }), ], }) export class AppModule {} Every config.get() above has a default, so no option ends up undefined. The next two sections explain why both details matter.

The dashboard routes are registered with RouterModule when the module is defined, which happens before your factory runs. That registration can only use the basePath you pass to forRootAsync() itself (default /telemetry). The basePath your factory returns is used afterwards, at request time, by the request watcher to skip the dashboard's own calls. Keep both values the same, as in the example, by reading them from one constant: basePath passed to forRootAsync basePath returned by the factory Dashboard served at Its own calls recorded as requests not set not set /telemetry no /admin/telemetry /admin/telemetry /admin/telemetry no not set /admin/telemetry /telemetry yes warning Returning a basePath only from the factory does not move the dashboard: it stays at /telemetry. The access token is still asked there, since the guard is bound to the dashboard's routes, wherever they are mounted.

The factory's result is merged over the defaults with an object spread, and watchers is merged the same way one level down: { ...DEFAULT_OPTIONS, ...options, watchers: { ...DEFAULT_OPTIONS.watchers, ...options.watchers } } A key that is absent keeps its default. A key that is present with the value undefined replaces the default with undefined. That is exactly what config.get('SOME_VARIABLE') returns for an unset variable. Current limitation An option set to undefined is not ignored. Depending on the option: ignoredPrefixes: undefined makes the request watcher throw on every request: every route of your app answers 500. basePath: undefined (in forRoot()) or a missing basePath next to a factory value leaves the dashboard where you do not expect it. pruneHours: undefined or NaN makes each prune run delete every in-memory entry; pruneIntervalMs or flushIntervalMs set to undefined makes the timers fire every millisecond; maxEntries: NaN removes the per-type cap. accessToken: undefined silently leaves the dashboard open. watchers.mail: undefined is the only value read as "keep the default". Two ways to stay safe: Give every config.get() a default, as in the example above, or use getOrThrow() for values that must be set (an access token outside your machine). Drop undefined values before returning: src/telemetry.options.ts import { TelemetryModuleOptions } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; export function definedOnly(options: TelemetryModuleOptions): TelemetryModuleOptions { return Object.fromEntries( Object.entries(options).filter(([, value]) => value !== undefined), ) as TelemetryModuleOptions; } useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => definedOnly({ accessToken: config.get('TELEMETRY_TOKEN'), storage: config.get('TELEMETRY_STORAGE'), }), Numeric values read from the environment are strings: convert them with Number() and keep a default, as the example does for pruneHours.

The factory runs once, while the application starts. Changing an environment variable afterwards has no effect until the next start. The resolved options are held under the TELEMETRY_OPTIONS token inside the module; that token is not exported to the rest of your app.

You need one package, @nestjs-telemetry/core. Add @nestjs-telemetry/typeorm or @nestjs-telemetry/prisma when you also want SQL queries and entity changes recorded. Check the requirements first: Node.js 18 or later, NestJS 10 or 11, and the Express adapter.
npm npm install @nestjs-telemetry/core yarn yarn add @nestjs-telemetry/core pnpm pnpm add @nestjs-telemetry/core Then register the module in your root module: see Quick start.

Install the package that matches your ORM, next to the core package. TypeORM npm install @nestjs-telemetry/typeorm yarn add @nestjs-telemetry/typeorm pnpm add @nestjs-telemetry/typeorm Prisma npm install @nestjs-telemetry/prisma yarn add @nestjs-telemetry/prisma pnpm add @nestjs-telemetry/prisma Run only the line for your package manager. Registering them is covered in TypeORM and Prisma.

Peer dependencies are packages the telemetry packages use but expect your application to provide. A NestJS application already has everything the core package asks for. Package Peer dependency Accepted versions core @nestjs/common ^10.0.0 or ^11.0.0 core @nestjs/core ^10.0.0 or ^11.0.0 core reflect-metadata ^0.1.13 or ^0.2.0 core rxjs ^7.0.0 typeorm @nestjs-telemetry/core ^0.1.0 or ^0.2.0 typeorm @nestjs/common, @nestjs/core ^10.0.0 or ^11.0.0 typeorm @nestjs/typeorm ^10.0.0 or ^11.0.0 typeorm typeorm ^0.3.0 or ^1.0.0 prisma @nestjs-telemetry/core ^0.1.0 or ^0.2.0 prisma @nestjs/common, @nestjs/core ^10.0.0 or ^11.0.0 prisma @prisma/client ^5.0.0 or ^6.0.0 When one of your versions falls outside a range, npm 7 and later stops with an ERESOLVE error instead of installing. The repository's tests run against NestJS 10, TypeORM 0.3 with @nestjs/typeorm 10, and Prisma Client 5. The other versions in these ranges are accepted but not tested there.

The core package.json also marks @nestjs/schedule, @nestjs/cache-manager, @nestjs/event-emitter and @nestjs-modules/mailer as optional peers in peerDependenciesMeta. No code in the package imports them, so you never install them for the sake of telemetry. The same goes for nodemailer: mail capture instruments the transporters your application already creates.

The core package has two regular dependencies: uuid and better-sqlite3 (^11.0.0), the driver behind the SQLite storage. Because better-sqlite3 is a regular dependency, it is installed even when you keep the default in-memory storage. better-sqlite3 is a native addon. Its install script runs prebuild-install || node-gyp rebuild --release: prebuild-install downloads a prebuilt binary for your operating system, CPU architecture and Node.js version from the GitHub releases of better-sqlite3. If no binary matches, or the download is blocked, node-gyp compiles the addon from source. That needs Python 3, make and a C++ compiler: build-essential on Debian and Ubuntu, the Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS, or Visual Studio Build Tools with the C++ workload on Windows. If both steps fail, the whole install fails, whichever storage you use. At runtime the binary is loaded only when the SQLite storage is created, that is, with storage: 'sqlite'. The in-memory storage never loads it, so an application on the default storage starts even if the binary is missing or was built for another Node.js version.

With storage: 'sqlite', a missing or mismatched binary stops the application at startup. These are the usual causes: pnpm skipped the build. pnpm 10 and later do not run the install scripts of dependencies until you approve them. Run pnpm approve-builds and allow better-sqlite3, then reinstall. The error mentions Could not locate the bindings file. Node.js changed after the install. The binary is built for one Node.js version. Run npm rebuild better-sqlite3 after switching versions. The error mentions was compiled against a different Node.js version. The image changed. In a Docker build, install dependencies in an image with the same operating system and C library as the one that runs the application. A binary built on a Debian-based image does not load on Alpine.
