documents.t: The packages ship CommonJS compiled for ES2022, with type declarations. They need nothing beyond what NestJS needs: experimentalDecorators and emitDecoratorMetadata, which the tsconfig.json generated by the Nest CLI already sets. tsconfig.json { "compilerOptions": { "experimentalDecorators": true, "emitDecoratorMetadata": true } } emitDecoratorMetadata is what lets Nest inject a watcher by its class, as in constructor(private readonly mailWatcher: TelemetryMailWatcher). Tokens such as TELEMETRY_STORAGE are injected with @Inject(). The public declarations reference only @nestjs/common and rxjs, so you need no extra @types package, with or without skipLibCheck.

A common setup keeps the dashboard in development and staging and out of production. Install the package as a development dependency: npm npm install --save-dev @nestjs-telemetry/core yarn yarn add --dev @nestjs-telemetry/core pnpm pnpm add --save-dev @nestjs-telemetry/core A production install that omits development dependencies does not contain the package: Package manager Production install npm npm ci --omit=dev yarn (classic) yarn install --production pnpm pnpm install --prod In that install, a static import { TelemetryModule } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core' makes the application crash at boot with Cannot find module. Load the package at runtime instead, and only outside production: src/telemetry.imports.ts import type { DynamicModule, Type } from '@nestjs/common'; // A type-only import is erased by the compiler: it never loads the package at runtime. import type * as Telemetry from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; export function telemetryImports(): Array<Type<unknown> | DynamicModule> { if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') return []; let telemetry: typeof Telemetry; try { telemetry = require('@nestjs-telemetry/core'); } catch (err) { // Not installed (a production install without devDependencies): run without it. if ((err as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND') return []; throw err; } return [telemetry.TelemetryModule.forRoot()]; } src/app.module.ts import { Module } from '@nestjs/common'; import { telemetryImports } from './telemetry.imports'; @Module({ imports: [ // ...your other modules ...telemetryImports(), ], }) export class AppModule {} How this behaves: Two independent guards. The NODE_ENV check keeps the module off in production even when the package happens to be installed; the require() check keeps a production install without it bootable. Nest does not set NODE_ENV for you, so use whatever variable your deployment sets. Only a missing package is tolerated. Any other error thrown while loading the package still stops the boot. Value imports defeat it. import type is erased at compile time, but a value import from the package anywhere in code that runs in production, such as import { TELEMETRY_STORAGE } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core' in a service, loads it again and crashes the same way. Linting. If your ESLint configuration forbids require() (typescript-eslint's no-require-imports rule), disable that rule on the require() line. Pass options to forRoot() inside the helper as usual. To read them from ConfigService, return TelemetryModule.forRootAsync(...) from the helper instead: see Async configuration.

Install the ORM package as a development dependency too, and load it the same way: TypeORM. TelemetryTypeOrmModule is a plain module. Load @nestjs-telemetry/typeorm with require() in the same helper and add its TelemetryTypeOrmModule to the returned array, after TelemetryModule.forRoot(). Prisma. The middlewares are registered in your own PrismaService, which receives the storage through the TELEMETRY_STORAGE token. When the telemetry module is not loaded, that provider does not exist. Inject it with @Optional() @Inject('TELEMETRY_STORAGE'), where 'TELEMETRY_STORAGE' is the value of the exported constant (importing the constant would load the package), register the middlewares only when the storage is defined, and load @nestjs-telemetry/prisma with require() inside that branch.
documents.s: ORM packages in a development-only setup

documents.t: This page takes you from an existing NestJS application to a dashboard that shows its requests. It assumes the package is installed (Installation) and that the app uses the default Express adapter.

Import TelemetryModule.forRoot() once, in your root module: src/app.module.ts import { Module } from '@nestjs/common'; import { TelemetryModule } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; @Module({ imports: [TelemetryModule.forRoot()], }) export class AppModule {} The module is global: every other module can inject what it exports (the storage and the watchers) without importing it again. With no options, entries are kept in memory, the dashboard is served at /telemetry, and it has no access token. Every option is described in the Options reference.
npm run start:dev Open http://localhost:3000/telemetry (use your app's port). The page shows a sidebar with one view per entry type and a home view with counters and the last requests.
documents.s: 2. Start the app and open the dashboard

documents.t: Call any route of your app, from a browser, curl or your frontend: curl http://localhost:3000/ Within five seconds (the dashboard refreshes on its own) the request appears in Requests: method, path, status and duration. Click it to see the headers, the request body, the response body and every entry recorded while that request was handled. Using the dashboard walks through every view.

Watcher With forRoot() alone Requests Yes. A global interceptor records every HTTP request that reaches an interceptor. Exceptions Yes. A global interceptor records every error thrown by a handler or a pipe, and re-throws it. Mail Yes, for nodemailer transporters and the MailerService of @nestjs-modules/mailer that are providers, or fields of a provider, when the app starts. See Mail. Cache Yes, but see the warning on Cache: it does not observe a real cache. Logs No. Install TelemetryLogWatcher as a logger: see Logs. Schedules No. Run each job through TelemetryScheduleWatcher.wrap(): see Schedules. Events No. Call TelemetryEventWatcher.record() from your listeners: see Events. Queries and models No. Add the TypeORM or Prisma package.
documents.s: What works with no extra code

documents.t: Current limitation The request, exception and cache interceptors are bound to every route of the application and assume an HTTP request. In an application that also serves GraphQL, every top-level resolver fails with a TypeError once the module is imported, and microservice (RPC) handlers produce empty REQUEST entries. Use the package in HTTP-only applications for now. Global prefix. If main.ts calls app.setGlobalPrefix('api'), the dashboard moves to /api/telemetry, and externalBasePath keeps its own calls out of the Requests view. Read Global prefix and externalBasePath. A global interceptor that wraps responses. If your app wraps every response (for example { data: ... }), the dashboard shows nothing until you exempt its routes: see Serving and embedding the dashboard. Anything beyond your machine. Set an access token first: Access token and security.
Read your options from configuration with Async configuration. Persist entries across restarts with the SQLite storage. Wire the watchers that need a line of code.

NestJS Telemetry is built for development and staging. It records request bodies, SQL parameters, log lines and mail, and its dashboard can delete data. Read this page before it runs anywhere real users reach.

The safest production setup is none: install the package as a development dependency and register the module only outside production, as shown in Development-only setup. Use a staging environment with test data for shared debugging.
documents.s: First: do you need it there?

documents.t: Set accessToken from a secret, read so that a missing value stops the boot (getOrThrow()). See Access token and security. Use a version after 0.2.3: up to 0.2.3 the token could be skipped with a case variant of the URL, under a global prefix without externalBasePath, and on Fastify. Block the dashboard path at the proxy for everyone outside your network, with a rule that ignores case, since Express routes /TELEMETRY to the dashboard too. Serve it over HTTPS only, and mask token= in proxy and access logs.

Review what is not masked: SQL parameters, Prisma arguments, exception messages, log lines, event payloads, mail addresses, URL paths, header values under innocent names. Turn off what you do not need: watchers: { cache: false } (the cache watcher only guesses), and do not wire logs, events or ORM watchers you will not read. Add paths you never want recorded (/auth, webhooks with signed payloads) to ignoredPrefixes, remembering they are plain string prefixes compared with the full path.

Memory storage: up to maxEntries entries per type, nine types. A request entry can hold two 10 KB bodies plus headers, a mail entry 50 KB of HTML. With the defaults, plan for tens of megabytes; lower maxEntries on small containers. SQLite storage: nothing caps the file but pruning. Set pruneHours to what you need, put the file on a persistent volume, and do not use a filtered search on a very large database: it scans the whole type synchronously. Never let a BigInt reach an entry with SQLite (Prisma or TypeORM bigint ids): it stops all writes. See Storage.

Each request: one entry, the response copied (up to 256 KB) and masked, headers and body masked. Usually well under a millisecond, but large JSON responses cost a parse and a serialization. Each open dashboard tab: three API calls every five seconds. GraphQL or microservice transports in the same app: do not import the module there yet (see Requests).

Watch GET {basePath}/api/status: the recording flag, counts per type, and storage size (bufferSize growing on SQLite means writes are failing). Remember the dashboard's Enabled button pauses recording for the whole app, and Clear all and Prune delete data for everyone. Each instance has its own entries; a load-balanced dashboard shows a different instance on each refresh.
The storage is injectable, so an end-to-end test can assert on what a request recorded: that it sent a mail, ran a query or raised an exception.

test/signup.e2e-spec.ts import { INestApplication } from '@nestjs/common'; import { Test } from '@nestjs/testing'; import request from 'supertest'; import { TELEMETRY_STORAGE, TelemetryEntryType, TelemetryStorage } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; import { AppModule } from '../src/app.module'; /** Polls until `done` holds: entries are written when a response ends, and SQLite buffers them. */ async function eventually<T>(read: () => Promise<T>, done: (value: T) => boolean, timeoutMs = 2000): Promise<T> { const deadline = Date.now() + timeoutMs; for (;;) { const value = await read(); if (done(value) || Date.now() > deadline) return value; await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 10)); } } describe('sign-up', () => { let app: INestApplication; let storage: TelemetryStorage; beforeAll(async () => { const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({ imports: [AppModule] }).compile(); app = moduleRef.createNestApplication(); await app.init(); storage = app.get(TELEMETRY_STORAGE); }); afterAll(() => app.close()); beforeEach(() => storage.clear()); it('sends a welcome mail in the same request', async () => { await request(app.getHttpServer()).post('/auth/signup').send({ email: 'ana@example.com' }).expect(201); const mails = await eventually( () => storage.getByType(TelemetryEntryType.MAIL, {}, 0, 10), (list) => list.length > 0, ); expect(mails[0].content).toMatchObject({ to: 'ana@example.com', status: 'sent' }); const related = await storage.getByBatchId(mails[0].batchId); expect(related.map((entry) => entry.type)).toContain(TelemetryEntryType.REQUEST); }); }); Notes: Keep the default in-memory storage in tests: nothing to clean up, and reads are immediate. A REQUEST entry is written when its response ends, which can be just after supertest resolves: poll as above rather than reading once. With a mocked mailer (jest.fn() or jest.spyOn), the mock is left as it is and your assertions keep working; a spy that calls through is still recorded at the transport. To replace the storage in a test, use .overrideProvider(TELEMETRY_STORAGE).useValue(...).
documents.s: Read entries in an e2e test

documents.t: The module starts two timers (prune and flush) when it is created. app.close() stops them, flushes SQLite and puts back what mail instrumentation replaced. A test file that creates an app and never closes it keeps Jest from exiting ("Jest did not exit one second after the test run has completed").

Unit tests that build a single provider with Test.createTestingModule({ providers: [...] }) do not import TelemetryModule and are unaffected. If your tests import AppModule, you can turn the automatic parts off with watchers: { requests: false, exceptions: false, cache: false, mail: false }, or register the module only when an environment variable allows it.
documents.s: Keep it out of unit tests

documents.t: packages/core/test/support/test-app.ts builds a real Nest application with the module installed (memory or SQLite, forRoot or forRootAsync, an optional global prefix) and exposes eventually(), waitForRequests() and a demo controller. It is a good template for testing integrations of your own.

A global prefix moved it. With app.setGlobalPrefix('api') the dashboard is at /api/telemetry. See Global prefix. forRootAsync with a custom path. The route uses the basePath passed to forRootAsync() itself, not the one your factory returns. See Async configuration. The module is not imported in the root module, or it is registered only under a condition that is false (a development-only setup with NODE_ENV=production).

A global interceptor wraps every response ({ data: ... }): the page finds its data one level too deep. Exempt the telemetry controller: see Serving and embedding. The API calls fail. Open the browser's network tab: a 403 means the page was opened without ?token=; a 401 comes from one of your own guards (next section); 404 on /api/... means a proxy does not forward the API path. The page is unstyled or inert: the CDN scripts were blocked (offline, or a Content-Security-Policy). See What it loads. Recording is paused: the counters stay at zero while requests come in. Click Enabled twice (the first click reports the real state), or POST /api/toggle.
documents.s: The dashboard loads but stays empty

documents.t: Your own global guard (an app-wide JWT guard) runs on the dashboard routes too, and the browser does not send a bearer token there. Let the dashboard path through your guard when accessToken is set: see Your own global guards.
documents.s: A 401 on the dashboard, with the right token

documents.t: accessToken is empty or undefined: an unset environment variable leaves the dashboard open, and nothing says so. Read it with getOrThrow() (see Set an access token). Version 0.2.3 or earlier: the guard compared paths, so a global prefix without externalBasePath, a basePath without its leading slash, a basePath returned only by the forRootAsync factory, a case variant of the URL (/TELEMETRY/api/...) and Fastify all skipped the token. Upgrade: the guard is now bound to the dashboard's routes (see Where the token is checked).
documents.s: The access token is not enforced

documents.t: Under a global prefix, set externalBasePath to the prefixed path, and write basePath with a leading slash and no trailing one (see Global prefix and externalBasePath).
documents.s: The dashboard's own calls fill the Requests view

documents.t: An option set to undefined, typically ignoredPrefixes: config.get('...') for an unset variable: see How options are merged. GraphQL resolvers fail with a TypeError in the request interceptor: the module supports HTTP-only apps for now. A body full of eyJ-like text used to block the event loop for seconds in the JWT masking; fixed in the current version, upgrade.
documents.s: Every route of my app answers 500 after adding the module

documents.t: See the checklist on Mail. The most common causes: a transporter created after startup, an HTTP API client instead of nodemailer, or application code that skips sending outside production.

They are not captured on their own: Logs: install a logger that forwards to TelemetryLogWatcher. See Logs. Schedules: wrap each job with TelemetryScheduleWatcher.wrap(). See Schedules. Events: call TelemetryEventWatcher.record(), or record every emission with onAny(). See Events.
documents.s: Logs, schedules or events do not show up

documents.t: You installed TelemetryLogWatcher directly with app.useLogger(). It records but does not print. Use the forwarding logger from Logs.

TypeORM older than 0.3.18 has no afterQuery event. Upgrade TypeORM. TelemetryTypeOrmModule is not imported, or your queries run on a named DataSource: only the default one is instrumented. Prisma: the middlewares must be registered with $use() in your PrismaService.
Prisma removed $use in 6.14. Use the client extension from Prisma, or stay below 6.14.
documents.s: Prisma: this.$use is not a function

documents.t: The Prisma middlewares copy arguments with JSON.stringify, which throws on BigInt, failing your query. Use the client extension from Prisma, which converts them.
documents.s: Prisma: "Do not know how to serialize a BigInt"

documents.t: See The native SQLite dependency: pnpm's build approval, a Node.js version change (npm rebuild better-sqlite3), or a Docker image mismatch.
documents.s: better-sqlite3 fails to install or load

documents.t: One entry could not be serialized (usually a BigInt id) and blocks every flush. GET /api/memory shows bufferSize growing while dbEntries stays still. Find what produces it (ORM entities with bigint keys), stop it, then restart the app; the blocked buffer is lost with the process.
documents.s: SQLite: the dashboard returns 500 and nothing new is stored

documents.t: Nothing caps it besides pruning. Lower pruneHours, check that the prune timer runs (pruneIntervalMs), or call POST /api/prune?hours=N.

The in-memory storage keeps up to maxEntries entries per type, nine types, each request with up to two 10 KB bodies. Lower maxEntries, turn off the cache watcher, and add noisy paths to ignoredPrefixes.

The user is read from req.user when the request reaches the interceptor: authentication that sets it later (inside the handler) is not seen. A user object without email, username, id or sub is recorded as [object Object]. With watchers.requests: false there is no request context at all.
Numeric ids are stored as numbers and the filter compares them with a string. Make req.user.id a string, or identify users by email or username.
An application created in a test was not closed: the prune and flush timers keep the process alive. Call await app.close() in afterAll.

@nestjs-telemetry/prisma ships two Prisma middlewares: one records every operation as a QUERY entry, the other records writes as MODEL entries. Prisma 6.14 and later The middlewares are registered with prisma.$use(), which Prisma deprecated in 4.16 and removed in 6.14 (it is not in Prisma 7 either). The package's peer range (^5.0.0 || ^6.0.0) accepts versions where this.$use is not a function and your PrismaService fails to start. The middlewares work with Prisma 5 and 6.0 to 6.13; the repository tests them with Prisma 5. For later versions, use the client extension below.

npm install @nestjs-telemetry/prisma src/prisma/prisma.service.ts import { Inject, Injectable, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common'; import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client'; import { TELEMETRY_STORAGE, TelemetryStorage } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; import { createTelemetryModelMiddleware, createTelemetryQueryMiddleware } from '@nestjs-telemetry/prisma'; @Injectable() export class PrismaService extends PrismaClient implements OnModuleInit { constructor(@Inject(TELEMETRY_STORAGE) storage: TelemetryStorage) { super(); this.$use(createTelemetryQueryMiddleware(storage)); this.$use(createTelemetryModelMiddleware(storage)); } async onModuleInit() { await this.$connect(); } } TelemetryPrismaModule is exported too, but it is an empty module: importing it does nothing.

Field Content model The Prisma model, or Unknown for raw queries. action findMany, create, update, upsert... type SELECT (find, count, aggregate, groupBy), INSERT (create...), UPDATE (update..., upsert), DELETE (delete...) or OTHER. duration Milliseconds. args The operation's arguments, copied through JSON. error The error message when the operation failed, else ''.

Recorded after a successful create, createMany, update, updateMany, upsert, delete or deleteMany. Field Content entity The model. action CREATED, UPDATED (upsert included) or DELETED. entityId result.id, else result.uuid, else '' (empty for the ...Many operations). data args.data, copied through JSON. Tags: model:<action> and entity:<Model>.

Current limitation A BigInt breaks your query. The arguments are copied with JSON.stringify, which throws on BigInt. A query with a BigInt argument then fails with that error, and for a write the error comes after the row was committed. A BigInt id returned by a write ends up stored as is, which breaks the SQLite storage (see Storage). Arguments are not masked: a password or token in data or where is stored as it is. The dashboard shows Prisma queries as blank rows and groups them all together: the Queries view reads the sql field, which Prisma entries do not have. Open an entry to see its model, action and arguments. watchers.queries and watchers.models are not read.

Until the package ships one, you can record the same entries with a Prisma client extension in your own code. The storage, the context and the entry types are public: src/prisma/telemetry.extension.ts import { Prisma } from '@prisma/client'; import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'; import { TelemetryContext, TelemetryEntryType, TelemetryStorage } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; const WRITES: Record<string, string> = { create: 'CREATED', createMany: 'CREATED', update: 'UPDATED', updateMany: 'UPDATED', upsert: 'UPDATED', delete: 'DELETED', deleteMany: 'DELETED', }; function sqlType(operation: string): string { if (/^(find|count|aggregate|groupBy)/.test(operation)) return 'SELECT'; if (operation.startsWith('create')) return 'INSERT'; if (operation.startsWith('update') || operation === 'upsert') return 'UPDATE'; if (operation.startsWith('delete')) return 'DELETE'; return 'OTHER'; } /** A JSON copy that turns BigInt into strings instead of throwing. */ function copy(value: unknown): unknown { return JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value ?? {}, (_key, v) => (typeof v === 'bigint' ? v.toString() : v))); } export function telemetryExtension(storage: TelemetryStorage) { const store = (type: TelemetryEntryType, content: Record<string, unknown>, tags: string[]) => { try { void storage.store({ uuid: randomUUID(), type, createdAt: new Date(), batchId: TelemetryContext.getBatchId() ?? '', content, userIdentifier: TelemetryContext.getUserIdentifier() ?? '', tenantId: TelemetryContext.getTenantId() ?? '', tags, }); } catch { // Recording must never change the query's outcome. } }; return Prisma.defineExtension({ name: 'nestjs-telemetry', query: { $allModels: { async $allOperations({ model, operation, args, query }) { if (!storage.isEnabled()) return query(args); const start = Date.now(); const type = sqlType(operation); let error = ''; try { const result = await query(args); const action = WRITES[operation]; if (action) { const row = result as { id?: unknown; uuid?: unknown } | null; const entityId = row?.id ?? row?.uuid ?? ''; store(TelemetryEntryType.MODEL, { entity: model, action, entityId: typeof entityId === 'bigint' ? entityId.toString() : entityId, data: copy((args as { data?: unknown }).data), }, [`model:${action.toLowerCase()}`, `entity:${model}`]); } return result; } catch (err) { error = err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err); throw err; } finally { store(TelemetryEntryType.QUERY, { model, action: operation, type, duration: Date.now() - start, args: copy(args), error, }, [`query:${type.toLowerCase()}`]); } }, }, }, }); } Provide the extended client from a factory, since $extends() returns a new client: src/prisma/prisma.module.ts import { Global, Module } from '@nestjs/common'; import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client'; import { TELEMETRY_STORAGE, TelemetryStorage } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; import { telemetryExtension } from './telemetry.extension'; export const PRISMA = Symbol('PRISMA'); @Global() @Module({ providers: [ { provide: PRISMA, inject: [TELEMETRY_STORAGE], useFactory: async (storage: TelemetryStorage) => { const client = new PrismaClient().$extends(telemetryExtension(storage)); await client.$connect(); return client; }, }, ], exports: [PRISMA], }) export class PrismaModule {} On Prisma 7, import Prisma and PrismaClient from the location your generator writes the client to. This extension is application code, not part of the package: it also fixes the BigInt problem above, but not masking.
documents.s: Prisma 6.14 and later: a client extension

documents.t: @nestjs-telemetry/typeorm attaches two TypeORM subscribers to your DataSource: one records every SQL query as a QUERY entry, the other records inserts, updates and removals as MODEL entries.

npm install @nestjs-telemetry/typeorm src/app.module.ts import { Module } from '@nestjs/common'; import { TypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs/typeorm'; import { TelemetryModule } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; import { TelemetryTypeOrmModule } from '@nestjs-telemetry/typeorm'; @Module({ imports: [ TypeOrmModule.forRoot({ /* your connection */ }), TelemetryModule.forRoot(), TelemetryTypeOrmModule, ], }) export class AppModule {} TelemetryTypeOrmModule injects the default DataSource (@InjectDataSource()) and the telemetry storage, and in its onModuleInit pushes its two subscribers onto dataSource.subscribers. It needs TypeOrmModule and TelemetryModule in the application. Peer dependencies: @nestjs/typeorm 10 or 11 and typeorm ^0.3.0 || ^1.0.0. Current limitation Queries are captured through TypeORM's afterQuery subscriber event, which exists from TypeORM 0.3.18. With an older 0.3.x, which the peer range accepts, no QUERY entry is ever recorded. Use TypeORM 0.3.18 or later.

Field Content sql The SQL as sent to the driver. type SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL (create/alter/drop) or OTHER. duration TypeORM's execution time in milliseconds (0 when it does not report one). parameters The bound parameters, as they are. Tags: query:<type>, for example query:select. Queries that contain telemetry_entries, plus SELECT 1 and SELECT version... health checks, are skipped.

TypeORM event action afterInsert CREATED afterUpdate UPDATED, with changedFields from TypeORM's updatedColumns afterRemove DELETED Field Content entity The entity's metadata name. action As above. entityId The entity's id, else its uuid, else ''. changedFields Property names (updates only). Tags: model:<action> and entity:<Name>. These events fire for save(), remove() and the other entity-manager operations that work on entities; entities whose name contains telemetry or telescope are skipped.

Only the default DataSource is instrumented. Queries of a named connection (TypeOrmModule.forRoot({ name: 'reports' })) are not recorded. Failed queries look successful: the entry has no error field and the duration TypeORM reported. Ids are guessed from id or uuid. Other primary key names, and operations without a loaded entity (a QueryBuilder or criteria update/delete), are recorded with an empty id; remove(entity) also records an empty id because TypeORM clears it. Parameters are not masked: a password hash or token bound to a query is stored as it is. watchers.queries and watchers.models are not read: to stop recording, do not import TelemetryTypeOrmModule. In the dashboard, the Models detail panel does not show the entity name, and different entities with the same id are grouped together.

NestJS Telemetry is a debugging dashboard you add to a NestJS application with one module import. While the application runs, watchers record what it does: HTTP requests and their responses, exceptions, SQL queries, log lines, scheduled jobs, cache lookups, events, mail and entity changes. The application itself serves a dashboard, at /telemetry by default, where you browse those entries as they arrive. If you know Laravel Telescope, this is the same idea for NestJS: no agent to run, no collector, no external service.

NestJS Telemetry is for developers who want to see what their application did, request by request, while they build and test it: the status and body a client received, the exception behind a 500, the queries and log lines a request produced, the mail it sent. It also works as a shared debugging view on a development or staging server. It is not an APM product or an OpenTelemetry SDK. It exports nothing: entries stay in the application's memory or in a local SQLite file, and the dashboard reads them from there.

Every entry has one of nine types. Each type is captured in one of three ways: Automatic: active as soon as you import TelemetryModule. Watcher call: you hand data to an injectable watcher from your own code. ORM package: you install and register @nestjs-telemetry/typeorm or @nestjs-telemetry/prisma. Type What is recorded How it is captured REQUEST Method, path, query string, status, duration, client IP, request and response headers and bodies (masked, then cut at 10,000 characters) Automatic. A global interceptor writes one entry per HTTP request when its response ends. See Requests. EXCEPTION Error class, message, stack trace (up to 5,000 characters), file and line, the request's method and path, cause Automatic. A global interceptor records any error thrown while a route handler runs (pipes included) and re-throws it unchanged. See Exceptions. QUERY TypeORM: SQL, statement type, duration, parameters. Prisma: model, action, statement type, duration, arguments, error ORM package. See TypeORM and Prisma. LOG Level, message, context, trace Watcher call. TelemetryLogWatcher is a LoggerService that you register with app.useLogger(). See Logs. SCHEDULE Class and method name, status (completed or failed), duration, error message Watcher call. You run each job body through TelemetryScheduleWatcher.wrap(). See Schedules. CACHE Key (ControllerName.handlerName), HIT or MISS, duration Automatic. A global interceptor records every route handler that returns a value. See Cache. EVENT Event name, payload, payload class, handler class and method Watcher call. You call TelemetryEventWatcher.record() from your listeners. See Events. MAIL Recipients, sender, subject, HTML and text bodies, a text preview, attachment names and sizes, sent or failed, error, duration, message id Automatic for nodemailer transporters and the MailerService of @nestjs-modules/mailer found among your providers at startup. Watcher call (TelemetryMailWatcher) for any other sender. See Mail. MODEL Entity, action (CREATED, UPDATED or DELETED), entity id, changed fields (TypeORM) or written data (Prisma) ORM package. See TypeORM and Prisma. Entries recorded while an HTTP request is handled share that request's batch ID, so the dashboard can list everything one request caused next to it. See Batch correlation. Current limitation Logs, scheduled jobs and events are not captured on their own. The module does not hook into Nest's logger, @nestjs/schedule or @nestjs/event-emitter, so those views stay empty until you wire the corresponding watcher. The cache watcher does not look at any cache. It records a CACHE entry for every route handler that returns a value, the dashboard's own API routes included, and labels it HIT when the handler took less than 2 ms and MISS otherwise.

Package Version What it adds @nestjs-telemetry/core 0.2.3 TelemetryModule, the request, exception, log, schedule, cache, event and mail watchers, in-memory and SQLite storage, the REST API and the dashboard. @nestjs-telemetry/typeorm 0.2.0 TelemetryTypeOrmModule, which attaches a query subscriber and an entity subscriber to your TypeORM DataSource. @nestjs-telemetry/prisma 0.1.0 createTelemetryQueryMiddleware() and createTelemetryModelMiddleware(), which you register on your PrismaClient with $use(). The versions are the ones in each package's package.json. Both ORM packages require the core package as a peer dependency, in the range ^0.1.0 or ^0.2.0.

TelemetryModule.forRoot() returns a global dynamic module. It creates the storage, binds three global interceptors (requests, exceptions, cache), registers the log, schedule, event and mail watchers as injectable providers, instruments the sendMail() of the mail senders it finds among your providers at startup, and mounts a controller at basePath that serves the dashboard page and a JSON API under {basePath}/api, behind a guard that checks the access token when you set one. While a request is handled, the request interceptor keeps a batch ID in AsyncLocalStorage, and every entry recorded in that async context carries it. A background service deletes entries older than pruneHours and flushes the SQLite write buffer. The dashboard is a single HTML page that calls the API every five seconds. Architecture describes each piece.

Requirement Details Node.js 18 or later. This is the engines field of the repository's root package.json. The published packages declare no engines field, so your package manager does not check it. NestJS 10 or 11. @nestjs/common and @nestjs/core are peer dependencies in the range ^10.0.0 or ^11.0.0, together with reflect-metadata (^0.1.13 or ^0.2.0) and rxjs (^7.0.0). The test suite runs on NestJS 10. HTTP adapter Express (@nestjs/platform-express, the Nest default). The dashboard route is written against Express's response object (res.type().send()), and the tests run on Express only. The access-token guard does not depend on the adapter: it reads only the token query parameter and the x-telemetry-token header. Native build tools Only when no prebuilt better-sqlite3 binary matches your platform. See The native SQLite dependency. Browser The dashboard page loads Tailwind CSS from cdn.tailwindcss.com and Alpine.js from cdn.jsdelivr.net, so the browser that opens it must be able to reach both. A Content-Security-Policy that your application sends on every response (from helmet, for example) applies to the dashboard page too. note Fastify is not covered by the test suite. Up to 0.2.3, the access-token guard read Express's req.path, which a Fastify request does not have, so on @nestjs/platform-fastify the token protected nothing. The guard no longer looks at the path.

NestJS Telemetry is built for development and staging. Before you run it anywhere else, know what it does by default: The dashboard and its API are open. With no accessToken, anyone who can reach the application can read every entry and call the API routes that clear entries or pause recording. See Access token and security. It keeps request and response headers and bodies. Credentials are masked by field name and by the shape of a JWT, which does not catch everything. See Data masking. Entries live in memory. The default storage keeps up to 1,000 entries per type, loses them when the process restarts, and holds them separately in each instance of a scaled-out application. Storage covers the SQLite alternative. Each request costs extra work. Text responses up to 256 KB are copied and masked before they are stored. To keep the package out of production installs, add it as a development dependency: see Development-only setup. If you run it beyond development, go through the Production checklist first.

Installation: package managers, peer dependencies, the native SQLite module and a development-only setup. Quick start: from forRoot() to your first request in the dashboard. Options reference: every option and its default. Watchers overview: what each watcher records and how to wire the ones that are not automatic. Using the dashboard: views, filters and the entry detail.

Everything the watchers write and the dashboard reads goes through the TelemetryStorage interface (see Public API). This page states the contract the two built-in storages share, so you can write, test or review another one.

Current limitation There is no supported way to plug your own storage into an application: the storage option accepts 'memory' or 'sqlite', and the TELEMETRY_STORAGE provider is defined inside the module, where an importing module cannot replace it. In tests you can replace it, since Nest's testing module can override any provider: const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({ imports: [AppModule] }) .overrideProvider(TELEMETRY_STORAGE) .useValue(new MyStorage()) .compile();

Method Must store(entry) Keep the entry. Do nothing while isEnabled() is false. Never throw for a valid entry; the watchers call it from inside your requests. getByType(type, filters, page, size) Return the entries of type matching filters, newest first, skipping page * size and returning at most size. Filter first, paginate second. Include entries not yet flushed. countByType(type, filters) Count with exactly the same predicate as getByType, so the dashboard's pager agrees with the pages. getByUuid(uuid) Return the entry or null, buffered entries included. getByBatchId(batchId) Return every entry with that batch, of every type, oldest first. getStats() Return a count per type, with a key for every TelemetryEntryType, buffered entries included. clear() / clearByType(type) Delete everything / every entry of one type, buffer included. pruneOlderThan(date) Delete entries with createdAt before date, buffer included; return how many. getDistinctTags(), getDistinctUserIdentifiers(), getDistinctTenantIds() Return sorted unique values, without ''. getMemoryInfo() Return any JSON object describing the storage; /api/memory and /api/status show it as is. isEnabled() / setEnabled(enabled) The recording flag behind the dashboard's Enabled button; start enabled. flush() Persist whatever is buffered; a no-op when nothing is. Called every flushIntervalMs and at shutdown.

Filter Matches when userIdentifier, tenantId The entry's field is equal. method content.method equals it, ignoring case. Entries without one never match. statusGroup `${Math.floor(content.status / 100)}xx` equals it (2xx...5xx). Entries without a status never match. search Some top-level value of content, converted with String(), contains it, ignoring case. All present filters must match.

Extending a built-in storage is the easiest way to add behavior, for example forwarding entries somewhere else as they arrive: src/telemetry/forwarding.storage.ts import { InMemoryTelemetryStorage, TelemetryEntry } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; export class ForwardingStorage extends InMemoryTelemetryStorage { constructor(private readonly forward: (entry: TelemetryEntry) => void, maxEntries = 1000) { super(maxEntries); } async store(entry: TelemetryEntry): Promise<void> { await super.store(entry); if (!this.isEnabled()) return; try { this.forward(entry); } catch { // A failing destination must not fail the request that produced the entry. } } }

The repository checks both storages against the same scenarios in packages/core/test/storage.consistency.spec.ts: 60 requests and a few logs, every filter combination, pages that must add up to the count, newest-first order. Run your implementation through the same scenarios: the fixtures are in packages/core/test/support/entries.ts.

The module mounts one controller at basePath (default /telemetry). The dashboard page is served at GET {basePath}; every JSON route is under {basePath}/api. Under a global prefix, both move with it: see Global prefix.

Envelope. Every JSON route answers: { "success": true, "message": "ok", "data": {} } Errors. A missing type or an unknown UUID answers success: false with HTTP 200 and data: null. Unexpected failures surface as Nest's 500. Authentication. With accessToken set, every route (the page included) needs the token, in the x-telemetry-token header or the token query parameter. Without it the answer is 403. See Access token and security. export T=your-token curl -H "x-telemetry-token: $T" http://localhost:3000/telemetry/api/stats

Method Path Purpose GET {basePath} The dashboard page (HTML) GET /api/entries List entries of one type GET /api/entries/:uuid One entry GET /api/entries/:uuid/related Entries of the same batch GET /api/filters Values for the filter dropdowns GET /api/stats Count per type GET /api/status Recording flag, counts and storage info GET /api/tags Every distinct tag GET /api/memory Storage info POST /api/toggle Pause or resume recording POST /api/flush Write the SQLite buffer now POST /api/prune Delete entries older than N hours POST /api/prune/expired Same, reported as retention DELETE /api/entries Delete entries of one type, or all Paths below are relative to {basePath}.

On a large SQLite database, method, statusGroup and search load the whole type into memory: see Storage. Without type: { "success": false, "message": "type parameter is required", "data": null }.
The entry as data, or { "success": false, "message": "Entry not found", "data": null }.
Every entry with the same batchId, oldest first. An unknown entry, or one without a batch, answers data: [].

{ "users": [{ "id": "ana@example.com", "name": "ana@example.com" }], "tenants": [{ "id": "t1", "name": "t1" }], "methods": ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"], "statuses": ["2xx", "3xx", "4xx", "5xx"] } users and tenants are the distinct values recorded so far, sorted.
A count per type, every type present: { "REQUEST": 12, "EXCEPTION": 1, "QUERY": 40, ... }. On SQLite it includes buffered entries.
{ "enabled": true, "stats": { "REQUEST": 12 }, "memory": { "type": "memory", "totalEntries": 53, "maxEntriesPerType": 1000, "enabled": true } }
The memory object above. In memory: type, totalEntries, maxEntriesPerType, enabled. On SQLite: type: "sqlite", bufferSize, dbEntries, totalEntries, enabled.
Every distinct tag, sorted: ["cache:miss", "exception:TypeError", "mail", "to:ana@example.com"].
Flips the recording flag and answers { "enabled": false }. While paused no watcher stores anything. It takes no body: two calls cancel out.
Writes the SQLite buffer now; answers message: "Buffer flushed" and the memory info. Nothing to do in memory.

Query parameter Default hours 24 Deletes every entry created more than hours ago and answers { "pruned": 37, "hours": 24 }. hours=0 (or anything that is not a positive number) is treated as 24. POST /api/prune/expired does the same and answers { "pruned": 37, "retentionHours": 24 }.

With ?type=MAIL, deletes the entries of that type; without type, deletes everything. Answers message: "Entries cleared", data: null. curl -X DELETE -H "x-telemetry-token: $T" "http://localhost:3000/telemetry/api/entries?type=CACHE" note The state-changing routes have no CSRF protection beyond the token. Without a token, any web page a developer visits can send these requests to a dashboard on localhost.

TelemetryCacheInterceptor is bound as a global interceptor and writes CACHE entries. Current limitation The cache watcher does not observe any cache. For every route handler that returns a value, it records an entry labelled HIT when the handler took less than 2 ms and MISS otherwise. It also records the dashboard's own API calls, about three every five seconds while the dashboard is open. The labels say nothing about @nestjs/cache-manager or any other cache.
Field Content operation HIT (under 2 ms) or MISS. key ControllerName.handlerName. cacheName Always ''. duration Milliseconds the handler took. Tags: cache:hit or cache:miss.
Until the watcher observes a real cache, most applications are better off without it: TelemetryModule.forRoot({ watchers: { cache: false } });

The storage is injectable, so you can write accurate CACHE entries where your code talks to the cache. A small helper around cache-manager: src/common/telemetry-cache.ts import { CACHE_MANAGER } from '@nestjs/cache-manager'; import { Inject, Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; import type { Cache } from 'cache-manager'; import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'; import { TELEMETRY_STORAGE, TelemetryContext, TelemetryEntryType, TelemetryStorage, } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; @Injectable() export class TelemetryCache { constructor( @Inject(CACHE_MANAGER) private readonly cache: Cache, @Inject(TELEMETRY_STORAGE) private readonly storage: TelemetryStorage, ) {} async get<T>(key: string, cacheName = 'default'): Promise<T | undefined> { const start = Date.now(); const value = await this.cache.get<T>(key); if (this.storage.isEnabled()) { const operation = value === undefined || value === null ? 'MISS' : 'HIT'; void this.storage.store({ uuid: randomUUID(), type: TelemetryEntryType.CACHE, createdAt: new Date(), batchId: TelemetryContext.getBatchId() ?? '', content: { operation, cacheName, key, duration: Date.now() - start }, userIdentifier: TelemetryContext.getUserIdentifier() ?? '', tenantId: TelemetryContext.getTenantId() ?? '', tags: [`cache:${operation.toLowerCase()}`], }); } return value ?? undefined; } } The dashboard's Cache view shows these entries like the built-in ones, with your cache name and key, and links them to the request that made the lookup.

TelemetryEventWatcher.record() stores an EVENT entry: the event name, its payload and the handler that received it. Current limitation Events are not captured on their own: the watcher does not hook into @nestjs/event-emitter. An event appears in the dashboard only when your code calls record().

src/orders/order-created.listener.ts import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; import { OnEvent } from '@nestjs/event-emitter'; import { TelemetryEventWatcher } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; import { OrderCreatedEvent } from './order-created.event'; @Injectable() export class OrderCreatedListener { constructor(private readonly events: TelemetryEventWatcher) {} @OnEvent('order.created') async handle(event: OrderCreatedEvent) { await this.events.record('order.created', event, OrderCreatedListener.name, 'handle'); // ...your handling } } The signature is record(eventName: string, payload: any, handlerClass: string, handlerMethod: string): Promise<void>.

To see every event without touching each listener, record emissions instead, with EventEmitter2.onAny(): src/telemetry/event-recorder.ts import { Injectable, OnModuleInit } from '@nestjs/common'; import { EventEmitter2 } from '@nestjs/event-emitter'; import { TelemetryEventWatcher } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; @Injectable() export class EventRecorder implements OnModuleInit { constructor( private readonly emitter: EventEmitter2, private readonly events: TelemetryEventWatcher, ) {} onModuleInit() { this.emitter.onAny((event, payload) => { void this.events.record(String(event), payload, 'EventEmitter2', 'emit'); }); } } onAny listeners run synchronously inside emit(), so an event emitted while handling a request carries that request's batch ID.

Field Content event The event name. eventClass The payload's constructor name (OrderCreatedEvent, Object, Array), or '' for a primitive. payload The payload after a JSON round trip: dates become strings, functions and undefined disappear. A primitive is stored as { value }, null or undefined as {}. handlerClass, handlerMethod The names you passed. Tags: event:<name>.

A payload that cannot be serialized (a BigInt anywhere in it, a circular reference) is replaced as a whole by { toString: String(payload) }. Payloads are stored whole: no size limit and no masking. Do not record events that carry secrets or large buffers. The dashboard's Events list shows the event name but not the handler (it reads a field the watcher does not write); the detail panel shows the payload. The watchers.events switch is not read.

TelemetryExceptionInterceptor is bound as a global interceptor. When a handler, or a pipe in front of it, throws, it records an EXCEPTION entry and re-throws the same error, so your exception filters and Nest's default handling run unchanged.

Field Content class The error's constructor name (NotFoundException, TypeError...), or UnknownError. message error.message, or String(error). Not masked. trace The stack trace, cut at 5,000 characters. file, line, location The first frame of the stack, when it has the (file:line:column) form. uri, method The request's path (or URL) and method. cause String(error.cause) when the error has a cause. Tags: exception:<ClassName>. The entry carries the request's batch ID, user and tenant, so it shows up next to the request in the dashboard.

Every error that reaches the interceptor, HttpExceptions included: a NotFoundException or a validation BadRequestException is recorded like a crash. Errors thrown before the interceptor chain (in middleware or guards) are not recorded, and neither are routes that match nothing. The request watcher records the same request with its final status, so a 500 appears in Requests and in Exceptions, linked by the batch.

recordException(storage, error, request) writes the same entry. Use it from your own exception filter, for errors handled outside a handler: src/all-exceptions.filter.ts import { ArgumentsHost, Catch, ExceptionFilter, HttpException, Inject } from '@nestjs/common'; import { TELEMETRY_STORAGE, TelemetryStorage, recordException } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; @Catch() export class AllExceptionsFilter implements ExceptionFilter { constructor(@Inject(TELEMETRY_STORAGE) private readonly storage: TelemetryStorage) {} catch(exception: unknown, host: ArgumentsHost): void { const http = host.switchToHttp(); recordException(this.storage, exception, http.getRequest()); const status = exception instanceof HttpException ? exception.getStatus() : 500; http.getResponse().status(status).json({ statusCode: status }); } } recordException returns nothing and does not wait for the storage; it skips recording while recording is paused. If the global interceptor already saw the same error, both entries are kept.

TelemetryExceptionFilter is exported for scoped use, but avoid it: Current limitation The filter re-throws the exception from catch(). Registered by class (@UseFilters(TelemetryExceptionFilter)), Nest cannot resolve its constructor argument and the app fails at startup; registered as an instance, the re-thrown error escapes Nest's exception layer and can crash the process. Record from your own filter with recordException() instead, as above.
watchers: { exceptions: false } binds a pass-through interceptor instead.

TelemetryLogWatcher is a Nest LoggerService that stores every line it receives as a LOG entry. It is not installed for you: the module registers it as an injectable, and you decide how log lines reach it.

Field Content level LOG, ERROR, WARN, DEBUG or VERBOSE. message The message, or JSON.stringify(message) when it is not a string. context The second argument of the call (the context, for Logger instances). trace For error(), its second argument (the stack). Tags: log:<level>, for example log:error. A line logged while a request is handled carries that request's batch ID, so it appears with the request in the dashboard.

The watcher only records: it never prints. Installing it directly with app.useLogger(app.get(TelemetryLogWatcher)) replaces Nest's logger, so your console goes silent. Install a logger that does both instead: src/telemetry-console.logger.ts import { ConsoleLogger } from '@nestjs/common'; import { TelemetryLogWatcher } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; /** Prints like Nest's ConsoleLogger and records every line in the telemetry dashboard. */ export class TelemetryConsoleLogger extends ConsoleLogger { constructor(private readonly telemetry: TelemetryLogWatcher) { super(); } log(message: any, ...params: any[]) { super.log(message, ...params); this.telemetry.log(asText(message), contextOf(params)); } warn(message: any, ...params: any[]) { super.warn(message, ...params); this.telemetry.warn(asText(message), contextOf(params)); } debug(message: any, ...params: any[]) { super.debug(message, ...params); this.telemetry.debug(asText(message), contextOf(params)); } verbose(message: any, ...params: any[]) { super.verbose(message, ...params); this.telemetry.verbose(asText(message), contextOf(params)); } error(message: any, ...params: any[]) { super.error(message, ...params); this.telemetry.error(asText(message), stackOf(message, params), contextOf(params)); } fatal(message: any, ...params: any[]) { super.fatal(message, ...params); this.telemetry.error(asText(message), stackOf(message, params), contextOf(params)); } } function asText(message: unknown): string { if (message instanceof Error) return message.message; if (typeof message === 'string') return message; try { return JSON.stringify(message, (_key, value) => (typeof value === 'bigint' ? value.toString() : value)); } catch { return String(message); } } /** Nest passes the context last. */ function contextOf(params: unknown[]): string | undefined { const last = params[params.length - 1]; return typeof last === 'string' ? last : undefined; } function stackOf(message: unknown, params: unknown[]): string | undefined { if (message instanceof Error) return message.stack; return params.length > 1 && typeof params[0] === 'string' ? params[0] : undefined; } src/main.ts import { NestFactory } from '@nestjs/core'; import { TelemetryLogWatcher } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; import { AppModule } from './app.module'; import { TelemetryConsoleLogger } from './telemetry-console.logger'; async function bootstrap() { // bufferLogs holds the startup lines until the logger below is installed, then replays them. const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, { bufferLogs: true }); app.useLogger(new TelemetryConsoleLogger(app.get(TelemetryLogWatcher))); await app.listen(3000); } bootstrap(); Every Logger instance in your app (new Logger(MyService.name)) now prints and records.
documents.s: Install it and keep the console

documents.t: Set basePackage to record only the lines whose context starts with a given string: TelemetryModule.forRoot({ basePackage: 'Orders' }); With that, new Logger('OrdersService').log(...) is recorded and Nest's own RouterExplorer or InstanceLoader lines are not. A line without a context is always recorded. The comparison is a plain, case-sensitive startsWith.

Current limitation Calling the watcher directly, without the wrapper above: logger.error(err) with an Error object records {}: the message and stack are lost. A message that cannot be serialized (a BigInt, a circular object) throws a TypeError back into the code that logged it. With basePackage set, a call whose second argument is not a string (logger.log('saved', { id })) throws a TypeError into your code. fatal() and setLogLevels() are not implemented, and messages are stored whole, with no size limit and no masking. The dashboard's log detail panel does not show the context or the trace (it reads other field names); the list shows level and message. Lines logged by middleware, guards or exception filters run outside the request's batch and are not linked to it. The watchers.logs switch is not read: to stop recording logs, stop forwarding them.

Mail is captured automatically. When the application starts, the module looks for the mail senders it knows among your providers and records every message they send, or fail to send. You do not call anything.

Sender Found when A nodemailer transporter (nodemailer.createTransport(...), nodemailer 6 or later) It is a provider itself, or a field of a provider or controller (directly, or as a value of a Map field). The MailerService of @nestjs-modules/mailer It is a provider. Its transporters are instrumented, including the ones addTransporter() adds later. The search runs once, in onApplicationBootstrap: after every module's onModuleInit, so a transporter created there is found. Both usual wirings work as they are: A transporter that is a provider @Module({ providers: [ { provide: 'MAIL_TRANSPORTER', inject: [ConfigService], useFactory: (config: ConfigService) => nodemailer.createTransport({ host: config.get('MAIL_HOST'), port: 587, auth: { user: config.get('MAIL_USER'), pass: config.get('MAIL_PASS') } }), }, EmailService, ], }) export class EmailsModule {} A transporter kept in a field @Injectable() export class EmailService { private readonly transporter = nodemailer.createTransport({ host: 'smtp.example.com', port: 587 }); sendWelcome(to: string) { return this.transporter.sendMail({ from: 'noreply@example.com', to, subject: 'Welcome', html: '

Hi

' }); } } Not found: a transporter created later (inside a method, or on first use), one kept deeper than one property, one in a #private field, or one owned by a request-scoped provider. For those, see Senders the module cannot see.

The message is recorded where nodemailer hands it to its transport, so the entry shows what was really sent: a template already rendered into HTML, the transporter's defaults (such as from) applied, the recipients after any interception. Field Content to, from, cc, bcc, replyTo Addresses as one line: Ana <ana@example.com>, bob@example.com. Empty ones are left out. subject The subject. type html or text. bodyPreview The text a reader sees, without markup, styles or scripts: the first 500 characters. html The HTML, up to 50 KB; htmlTruncated: true when it was longer. text The plain-text body, up to 10,000 characters. template The template name, for @nestjs-modules/mailer. attachments { filename, contentType, size } per attachment (20 at most). Their content is never stored. status sent or failed. error Why it failed. duration Milliseconds from sendMail() to the transport's answer. messageId The Message-ID. accepted, rejected The recipients the transport reported. transport SMTP, SMTP (pool), SESTransport, JSONTransport... source nodemailer, mailer or manual. Tags: mail, one to:<address> per recipient, and mail:failed for a failure. A mail sent while handling a request carries that request's batch ID, user and tenant, even when the transport answers later from a pooled connection opened by another request.

Two kinds of failure are recorded, both with status: 'failed' and the error message: the transport refused or could not deliver (authentication, connection, rejected recipients); the message failed before reaching the transport (a template that does not exist, an invalid address). The entry is then built from the options passed to sendMail(). Your code receives exactly the same result or error as without telemetry.

The Mail view lists subject and recipients, with a FAILED badge on failures. The detail panel shows the status, duration and transport, the error, every address, the message id, rejected recipients, attachments, the HTML rendered in a sandboxed frame, and the text preview. The frame runs no script, submits no form and cannot navigate the dashboard. Remote images and fonts are blocked, so opening a mail fires no tracking pixel; Load them lifts the block for that mail.

Mail bodies have no field names, so they are masked by what can be recognised: every JWT by its shape, and the query string and fragment of every link, href attributes included, the way a request's query string is (https://app/reset?token=... keeps the address and loses the token). A link carried inside another link's query string is masked too. A code written in the text itself ("your code is 123456") is not masked, and neither are addresses. See Data masking.

Inject TelemetryMailWatcher (the module exports it). A nodemailer-style sender created later: hand it to instrument(), which returns it. const transporter = this.mailWatcher.instrument(nodemailer.createTransport(smtpOptions)); await transporter.sendMail({ from, to, subject, html }); instrument() accepts a nodemailer transporter, a MailerService, or any object with nodemailer's sendMail(options, callback?) contract. Calling it twice changes nothing, and a jest mock passed to it is left untouched. An HTTP API client (Resend, SendGrid, the AWS SDK): call record() once the send settled. src/mail/resend-mail.service.ts import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; import { Resend } from 'resend'; import { TelemetryMailWatcher } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; @Injectable() export class ResendMailService { private readonly resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY); constructor(private readonly mailWatcher: TelemetryMailWatcher) {} async send(to: string, subject: string, html: string): Promise<void> { const from = 'Acme <noreply@example.com>'; const started = Date.now(); const { data, error } = await this.resend.emails.send({ from, to, subject, html }); await this.mailWatcher.record({ from, to, subject, html, status: error ? 'failed' : 'sent', error: error?.message, messageId: data?.id, duration: Date.now() - started, transport: 'Resend', }); if (error) throw new Error(error.message); } } record() takes a MailInfo: every field is optional, addresses may be strings, { name, address } objects or arrays, and the body can be given as html, text or body (with type). It never throws.

A jest.spyOn(transporter, 'sendMail') or a jest.fn() stays what it is, so your assertions keep working; a spied transporter's sends are still recorded at its transport. Two applications created in the same process that share a transporter each record their own mail while they are open, and the original methods are put back when the last one closes.
watchers: { mail: false } skips the search, and record() and instrument() do nothing.

Is the sender found? It must be a provider, or a field of one, when the app starts. A transporter created on first use needs instrument(); an API client needs record(). Did the application send anything? Code that skips sending outside production (returning a development code instead of mailing it, say) leaves nothing to record, which is common exactly where the dashboard runs. Is recording paused? Check the Enabled button. Is watchers.mail false? Which version? Up to 0.2.3, mail was recorded only by explicit record() calls.

A watcher turns something your application does into a telemetry entry. There are nine entry types, one per watcher. Type Watcher How it is captured Switch Page REQUEST TelemetryRequestInterceptor Automatic: global interceptor requests Requests EXCEPTION TelemetryExceptionInterceptor Automatic: global interceptor exceptions Exceptions CACHE TelemetryCacheInterceptor Automatic: global interceptor cache Cache MAIL TelemetryMailWatcher Automatic for nodemailer and MailerService; record() for anything else mail Mail LOG TelemetryLogWatcher You install it as the app logger none Logs SCHEDULE TelemetryScheduleWatcher You wrap each job with wrap() none Schedules EVENT TelemetryEventWatcher You call record() from listeners none Events QUERY TypeORM subscriber / Prisma middleware ORM package none TypeORM, Prisma MODEL TypeORM subscriber / Prisma middleware ORM package none TypeORM, Prisma "none" means the switch exists in TelemetryWatcherOptions but is not read: see Watcher toggles.

Every entry is a TelemetryEntry: Field Meaning uuid Unique id of the entry. type One of the nine types above. createdAt When it was recorded. batchId The batch it belongs to: the HTTP request (or scheduled run) it was recorded in, or ''. content The type-specific data. See Entry model for every field. userIdentifier, tenantId The user and tenant of the request, or ''. tags Short labels such as query:select or mail:failed. The batch ID is what links a request to the queries, logs, mail and exceptions it caused; see Batch correlation.

TelemetryModule is global and exports TelemetryLogWatcher, TelemetryScheduleWatcher, TelemetryEventWatcher, TelemetryMailWatcher and the TELEMETRY_STORAGE token. Inject them by class: import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; import { TelemetryEventWatcher } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; @Injectable() export class OrdersService { constructor(private readonly events: TelemetryEventWatcher) {} } Do not add these classes to your own module's providers: their constructors take the storage interface, which Nest cannot resolve by type, so listing them again fails dependency resolution. Use the instances the global module exports.

Paused means nothing is stored. Each watcher checks the storage's recording flag (the dashboard's Enabled button) before storing. Recording is a side effect. A watcher never changes your handler's arguments, result or error. Telemetry should not break the app. The request and mail watchers catch their own failures. Some other paths do not yet: the log watcher can throw on unusual arguments, and the Prisma middlewares can fail a query; those cases are listed on each page.
TelemetryRequestInterceptor is bound as a global interceptor (the outermost of the three the module binds) and records one REQUEST entry per HTTP request.

The entry is written when the response ends: on the Node response's finish event, or close if the connection closed first. That is the only moment the final status code is known: Nest sets 200/201 before the handler runs, and an exception filter writes the real 4xx/5xx after every interceptor has seen the error. If the response object cannot be observed, the entry is written when the handler settles instead.

Field Content method HTTP method. uri req.path (Express), or req.url when there is no path. queryString The query string, with sensitive parameters masked. status res.statusCode when the response ended. duration Milliseconds from the interceptor to the end of the response. ipAddress req.ip, or the socket's remote address. contentType, responseContentType Request and response Content-Type. requestHeaders, responseHeaders Every header, sensitive ones masked. requestBody The parsed body serialized and masked, then cut at 10,000 characters. A raw Buffer body is stored as [binary body omitted]. responseBody A copy of what was sent, masked, cut at 10,000 characters (rules below). The entry also gets the request's batchId, userIdentifier and tenantId. Its tags are empty.

The watcher wraps the response's write and end to copy what is sent, without changing it: the client always receives exactly what the handler or filter produced. Only text is kept: application/json, application/xml, +json/+xml types, and text/* except text/event-stream. A compressed response (Content-Encoding other than identity), a UTF-16 or UTF-32 charset, or binary content is stored as [non-text response omitted]. A response without a content type is kept only if it parses as JSON. More than 256 KB is not recorded: [response larger than 256 KB, not recorded]. HEAD, 204 and 304 responses have no body to record. A connection that closed before the response finished is marked [response incomplete: the connection closed first]. JSON is parsed and written back to be masked, so a number beyond 2^53 loses digits and a duplicated key collapses in the recorded copy. Masking rules: Data masking.

At the start of each request the watcher asks the user provider for the current user. The default, DefaultTelemetryUserProvider, reads req.user: userIdentifier is the first of email, username, id and sub that is set, or String(user); tenantId is req.user.tenantId. Interceptors run after guards, so a user set by a Passport guard is visible. There is no option to replace the user provider. Current limitation Identifiers are stored as they are. A numeric id or tenantId (or a user object without any of the four fields, recorded as [object Object]) makes the dashboard's user and tenant filters match nothing on the in-memory storage, because they compare a string from the query with a number.

Paths that start with the dashboard path (externalBasePath or basePath) or with one of ignoredPrefixes. Both are plain string prefixes: /health also skips /healthcare. Requests that never reach an interceptor: rejected by a guard (401/403), matching no route (404), or failing in middleware. They leave no REQUEST and no EXCEPTION entry. Everything while recording is paused. The duration starts at the interceptor, so time spent in middleware and guards is not included.

Current limitation The interceptor assumes an HTTP request on every route. In an app that also exposes GraphQL resolvers, each top-level resolver fails with a TypeError while the module is imported; microservice (RPC) handlers produce REQUEST entries with no method or path. Under Fastify, uri holds the raw URL with its query string, which is not masked there.
watchers: { requests: false } binds a pass-through instead. That also removes the batch context of every request: see Watcher toggles.

TelemetryScheduleWatcher.wrap() runs a function and records a SCHEDULE entry for it: how long it took and whether it failed. Use it in the body of your @Cron, @Interval and @Timeout methods. Current limitation Scheduled jobs are not captured on their own: the watcher does not hook into @nestjs/schedule. A job appears in the dashboard only when its body goes through wrap().

src/reports/reports.task.ts import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common'; import { Cron, CronExpression } from '@nestjs/schedule'; import { TelemetryScheduleWatcher } from '@nestjs-telemetry/core'; import { ReportsService } from './reports.service'; @Injectable() export class ReportsTask { constructor( private readonly schedules: TelemetryScheduleWatcher, private readonly reports: ReportsService, ) {} @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_HOUR) sendHourlyReport() { return this.schedules.wrap(ReportsTask.name, 'sendHourlyReport', () => this.reports.sendHourly()); } } The signature is wrap(className: string, methodName: string, fn: () => Promise<any>): Promise<any>. It returns what fn resolves to, and re-throws what it throws, after recording.

Field Content class, method The names you passed. status completed or failed. duration Milliseconds. exception The error message of a failed run, or ''. Tags: schedule:completed or schedule:failed. userIdentifier and tenantId are empty.

wrap() runs fn inside a new batch: the queries, log lines, mail and model changes of that run share its batch ID, and the dashboard lists them under the run. The batch is new even when wrap() is called while handling an HTTP request: the run is then not linked to that request. While recording is paused, wrap() just runs fn.
The Schedule view groups runs of the same class and method. A group shows the status of its newest run, so an older failure can hide behind a completed row: turn off Grouped to see every run.
